Marco conceptual para la aplicación del componente de reducción de amenazas de la medida de Reducción de Amenazas y Restauración de Especies (STAR) Resumen Uno de los objetivos principales del Marco Global de Biodiversidad de Kunming‐Montreal (KMGBF) es detener la extinción de especies y reducir el riesgo de extinción diez veces para 2050. Con el fin de garantizar que las medidas adoptadas en el marco de los objetivos del KMGBF contribuyan a reducir el riesgo de extinción de las especies, se diseñó el indicador «Reducción de amenazas y restauración de especies» (STAR), que permite establecer objetivos basados en la ciencia para las especies. STAR cuantifica la contribución potencial de las medidas de reducción de amenazas o de restauración del hábitat a la reducción del riesgo de extinción de las especies en una zona. Para apoyar la aplicación efectiva de STAR, desarrollamos un marco que permite pasar de determinar el componente de reducción de amenazas de STAR (START) con datos globales a calibrar START utilizando datos locales, para finalmente establecer objetivos y calcular las puntuaciones START reales para medir el progreso. El marco describe los enfoques específicos que pueden aplicarse para calcular estas diferentes métricas START. Primero, las puntuaciones estimadas de START utilizan datos globales para proporcionar una indicación inicial de las especies y las amenazas que se espera que estén presentes en una zona. A continuación, las puntuaciones calibradas de START implican confirmar la presencia local de especies y amenazas y los datos verificados a nivel local permiten establecer objetivos sólidos de mitigación de amenazas que pueden articularse como puntuaciones objetivo de START. El START calibrado también puede servir de base para la gestión reactiva y proactiva de las amenazas. Por último, se supervisan los cambios en la intensidad de las amenazas y se utilizan para calcular el START realizado. Para alcanzar el START realizado, los actores deben no solo reducir las amenazas existentes, sino también evitar que surjan nuevas amenazas en la zona.…
nb3c0655fe6ef: The mismatch between the scale of ecological processes and management decisions represents a significant challenge in marine conservation. This misalignment can result in ineffective conservation measures and compromise the sustainability of marine ecosystems. The large spatial resolution commonly used to analyze food webs may obscure key ecological processes and their functioning, leading to inaccurate conclusions with important consequences for management and governance. To address this gap, we used a food web indicator, the survey‐based mean trophic level (MTL), covering an entire bentho‐demersal community across four subregions of the Northeast Atlantic. The indicator was developed at two spatial resolutions, subregional and local (0.2° × 0.2° cells), and we used a long‐term dataset to assess food‐web status. A set of 18 ecological scenarios, based on different trophic level (TL) thresholds and depth ranges, were established for each subregion, and linear models were applied to the historical series for each scenario. At the subregional scale, the results indicated potential recovery of top predators in the northern area; however, the stable patterns under various scenarios may have been attributable to ongoing fishing pressure rather than to true ecosystem stability or a genuinely balanced state. At the finer spatial resolution, local declining trends were revealed that had been masked in the broader‐scale analysis. These contrasting patterns underscore the importance of spatial resolution when assessing the status of marine food webs and highlight the need to consider multiple ecological scenarios. We recommend aligning management strategies with the natural processes that govern marine ecosystems to enhance the resilience and long‐term sustainability of ocean environments. Evaluación y cuantificación de las variaciones en el funcionamiento de las redes tróficas a través de escalas Resumen El desajuste entre la escala de los procesos ecológicos y las decisiones de gestión es un reto importante para la conservación marina. Este desajuste puede dar lugar a medidas de conservación ineficaces y poner en peligro la sostenibilidad de los ecosistemas marinos. La alta resolución espacial que se suele emplear para analizar las redes tróficas puede ocultar procesos ecológicos clave y su funcionamiento, lo que lleva a conclusiones inexactas con importantes consecuencias para la gestión y la gobernanza. Para abordar este vacío, utilizamos un indicador de la red trófica, el nivel trófico medio (NTM) basado en estudios de campo, que abarca toda una comunidad bentónica y demersal en cuatro subregiones del Atlántico nororiental. El indicador se desarrolló en dos resoluciones espaciales, subregional y local (celdas de 0.2° x 0.2°), y con un conjunto de datos a largo plazo para evaluar el estado de las redes tróficas. Establecimos un conjunto de 18 escenarios ecológicos, basados en diferentes umbrales de nivel trófico (NT) y rangos de profundidad para cada subregión y se aplicaron modelos lineales a las series históricas de cada escenario. A escala subregional, los resultados indicaron una posible recuperación de los depredadores superiores en la zona norte; sin embargo, los patrones estables observados en diversos escenarios podrían deberse a la presión pesquera actual, más que a una verdadera estabilidad del ecosistema o a un estado genuinamente equilibrado. A una resolución espacial más detallada, se revelaron tendencias locales de declive que habían quedado ocultas en el análisis a mayor escala. Estos patrones contrastantes subrayan la importancia de la resolución espacial a la hora de evaluar el estado de las redes tróficas marinas y resaltan la necesidad de considerar múltiples escenarios ecológicos. Recomendamos armonizar las estrategias de gestión con los procesos naturales que rigen los ecosistemas marinos para mejorar la resiliencia y la sostenibilidad a largo plazo de los entornos oceánicos.
n968db71542d9: There is a persistent underrepresentation of marginalized voices in academic literature, including that for ecology and conservation. Such exclusion hampers career progression, perpetuating disadvantages for historically marginalized groups in the field, with implications for the direction of conservation research. Diverse perspectives foster novel thinking, strengthen innovation, and ensure research reflects the full spectrum of challenges faced by communities. To assess this underrepresentation, we analyzed self‐reported demographic data for authors of scientific articles to explore demographic trends and how they shifted between 2010 and 2020. The journals chosen were listed as conservation‐related by three or more of the five major journal indices. We used the same dimensions of diversity to assess editor demographics in 2021. In total, 2152 authors and 241 editors completed the survey (response rate: 21.5% authors; 29.5% editors). We found that overall author diversity across multiple traits (Rao's Q) increased between 2010 and 2020. Most notably, the representation of women increased from 29.5% to 35.6% of authors. However, women from lower‐middle‐ or low‐income countries still represented <1% of authors, and most dimensions of diversity saw little change over a decade. In 2020–2021, 80% of authors and 76% of editors self‐identified as White; over three‐quarters of respondents across years lived in high‐income countries; and nationals of three countries (the United Kingdom, the United States, and Australia) represented 34% of authors and 49% of editors (5% of the global population). Our study findings highlight the importance of considering intersectionality, as respondents spanning multiple marginalized identities were disproportionately underrepresented. Overall, our work highlights how a lack of representation continues to characterize academic publishing in conservation and ecology but shows signs of positive change. There is evidence that gender‐based initiatives are having a positive effect, yet more work is needed to enhance representation across other dimensions of diversity. Representación en la literatura sobre conservación Resumen Existe una infrarrepresentación persistente de las voces marginadas en la literatura académica, incluida la dedicada a la ecología y la conservación. Dicha exclusión dificulta el desarrollo profesional y perpetúa las desventajas para los grupos históricamente marginados en este ámbito, lo que tiene implicaciones para la orientación de la investigación en materia de conservación. La diversidad de perspectivas fomenta el pensamiento creador, refuerza la innovación y garantiza que la investigación refleje todo el espectro de retos a los que se enfrentan las comunidades. Para evaluar esta infrarrepresentación, analizamos los datos demográficos facilitados por los propios autores de artículos científicos con el fin de explorar las tendencias demográficas y cómo evolucionaron entre 2010 y 2020. Las revistas seleccionadas figuraban como relacionadas con la conservación en tres o más de los cinco principales índices de revistas. Utilizamos las mismas dimensiones de diversidad para evaluar los datos demográficos de los editores en 2021. En total, 2 152 autores y 241 editores completaron la encuesta (tasa de respuesta: 21,5 % de los autores; 29,5 % de los editores). Observamos que la diversidad general de los autores en múltiples características (Q de Rao) aumentó entre 2010 y 2020. Cabe destacar que la representación de las mujeres aumentó del 29,5 % al 35,6 % del total de autores. Sin embargo, las mujeres de países de renta media‐baja o baja seguían representando menos del 1 % de los autores, y en la mayoría de los aspectos relacionados con la diversidad apenas se observaron cambios a lo largo de la década.…
n963b4031cc22: Groundwater‐dependent pan wetlands are keystone habitats for aquatic biodiversity in semi‐arid landscapes, yet the processes that structure their invertebrate communities remain poorly resolved. We surveyed 221 pan wetlands across the Khakhea–Bray Transboundary Aquifer (KBTA), South Africa, a landscape of low relief (1027–1231 m a.s.l.), and asked whether macroinvertebrate assemblages track local physicochemical conditions, landscape position, or both. Pans were assigned to four elevation classes, used here as a surrogate for hydrogeomorphic setting and its hydroperiod consequences rather than as a climatic elevation gradient, because the total relief is an order of magnitude smaller than in studies where elevation acts as a direct driver. Waters were predominantly neutral to alkaline (mean pH 7.6–8.6), consistent with a strong groundwater signature. Dissolved oxygen, water temperature, water depth, ammonium, nitrate and phosphate differed significantly among classes, whereas pH, oxidation–reduction potential, conductivity, total dissolved solids and surface area did not. Assemblage composition differed among classes, but the effect was weak: global ANOSIM detected no separation, and similarity percentage analysis attributed between‐class dissimilarity (67.9%–73.4%) to shifts in the relative abundance of a few dominant taxa, chiefly Anostraca, Spinicaudata and Notostraca, rather than to species turnover. Taxa richness differed significantly among classes, whereas abundance, Simpson, Shannon–Wiener and evenness did not, and within‐class variation exceeded among‐class differences. Shallow, short‐hydroperiod pans were dominated by large branchiopods, whereas deeper, longer‐hydroperiod pans supported proportionally more predatory aquatic insects and molluscs, consistent with hydroperiod and predation, rather than elevation, acting as the operative filters. Boosted regression trees ranked geographic position, particularly longitude, above local physicochemical variables as a correlate of taxa richness; because the surveyed pans are strongly clustered in space, this result is interpreted as evidence of unmeasured, spatially structured habitat variation rather than as a predictive relationship. Conserving these systems will require maintaining groundwater regimes and the full range of hydroperiods across the pan network under coordinated transboundary management, and monitoring assemblage composition rather than richness alone.
n416eed9a8a69: Urbanization is expanding rapidly in tropical regions, yet its effects on the genetic structure and connectivity of invasive social insects remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated how urban and forest habitat contexts are associated with genetic diversity, population structure, and colony organization in the invasive termite Heterotermes tenuis (Hagen, 1858) across three paired urban‐forest sites in Guadeloupe, using 18 newly developed polymorphic microsatellite loci. A total of 414 workers from 50 nests were genotyped. Across habitats, we found no differences in allelic richness, observed heterozygosity, expected heterozygosity, or inbreeding coefficients, suggesting no generalized loss of neutral genetic diversity in urban populations. In contrast, analyses of population structure revealed significant genetic differentiation between urban and forest habitats within each site pair, with habitat explaining 14%–22% of the genetic variation. Isolation by distance was detected in only one site, and a landscape‐level MLPE model indicated that habitat context was a stronger predictor of genetic differentiation than geographic distance. Colony genetic structure was consistent across habitats: no mixed‐family nests were detected, and extended family colonies predominated in both urban and forest environments. Together, these results indicate that urban and forest populations maintain comparable neutral genetic diversity while exhibiting moderate habitat‐associated genetic structuring. However, because habitat type covaried with several environmental characteristics and historical introduction structure cannot be excluded, this differentiation cannot be attributed to urbanization alone. These findings highlight the importance of considering habitat‐associated genetic structure and colony organization when assessing the spread and management of invasive termites in tropical urban landscapes.
n13e662196db7: Antarctic toothfish (Dissostichus mawsoni) are a critical top fish predator in the Southern Ocean whose population dynamics are strongly influenced by a changing climate and fishing pressure. Their complex, long‐lived life history presents challenges to understanding their population dynamics that we endeavor to overcome through the use of both reduced‐representation sequencing and whole‐genome resequencing data from fish across different cohorts. Our unique sample set allowed us to compare genomic structure, diversity, and demographic changes between cohorts born before and after the year 2000, when changes to fisheries management practices in the Southern Ocean reduced incidences of illegal, unreported, and unregulated fishing. While our population structure analyses corroborate recent studies showing panmixia across circumpolar populations of D. mawsoni, comparisons between cohorts revealed key exceptions. A lack of admixture in fish born before 2000 contrasted with widespread admixture among post‐2000 individuals, consistent with increased mixing and/or genotype influx. Notably, genome‐wide diversity declined over time in the Ross Sea (management area 88), with significant losses observed in heterozygosity between pre‐2000 and post‐2000 cohorts. Elevated levels of inbreeding in the Ross Sea, coupled with evidence for recent population contraction from positive Tajima's D values, provided potential explanations for the observed reductions in genomic diversity. Our results reconcile circumpolar panmixia with localized erosion of diversity and elevated inbreeding in the Ross Sea sector, underscoring the value of temporal monitoring and the need to prioritize future research on the interplay between fisheries pressure and environmental change in driving population dynamics and genomic structure in exploited Southern Ocean species like toothfish.
n0175f4fadfb6: Ancient pathogen genomics and palaeoproteomics have transformed archaeological research on infectious disease by enabling the detection of pathogens, reconstruction of extinct lineages, and investigation of host responses in past populations. Yet pathogen identification alone addresses only part of retrospective diagnosis: whether an individual experienced disease, which tissues were affected, and how infection contributed to morbidity or death. Palaeoproteomics extends this enquiry through the recovery of pathogen proteins, host immune proteins, and tissue-associated molecules from ancient human remains and associated materials. This review evaluates its diagnostic contribution within the broader reconstruction of ancient disease ecology. Dental calculus provides a particularly rich record of oral host–microbe interactions, combining microbial signals with inflammatory and dietary proteins. Studies of mummified skin, muscle and other soft tissues, dental pulp, skeletal lesions, historical bloodstains, coprolites, and latrine residues further extend the range of evidence available for retrospective diagnosis. Protein-based investigations of intestinal infection also illustrate the need to distinguish antibody-based antigen detection from sequence-based proteomics. Published studies support several levels of inference, ranging from tissue identification and inflammatory processes to specific infection and, more cautiously, clinical disease. They also reveal continuing challenges involving peptide specificity, contamination, source attribution, and the interpretation of disease-associated proteins. Retrospective diagnosis is strongest when molecular findings are consistent with anatomical, archaeological, and historical evidence and help discriminate among plausible alternative diagnoses. Protein evidence therefore contributes not only to individual palaeopathological diagnosis but also to broader reconstructions of relationships among infection, diet, sanitation, care, and social conditions. Future progress will depend on comparative samples with and without independently supported pathological evidence, archaeological validation of diagnostic markers, transparent reporting, broader regional coverage, and sampling of finite human remains.
nc545f8543f9e: Accurate mapping of woody biomass and its temporal change is critical for understanding the global carbon balance, informing restoration and supporting evidence‐based policy on climate mitigation and livelihoods. The vegetation of the dry tropics, comprised largely of dry forests and savannas, holds substantial woody carbon stocks, but both stocks and change over time remain uncertain. Where Earth Observation (EO) data have been used to estimate change over time, different products give conflicting results on the direction, magnitude and location of change. We present pan‐dry‐tropical maps of aboveground carbon density (AGCD) and AGCD change at 100 m resolution for the years 2015–2024, developed using ALOS ScanSAR satellite radar observations calibrated with in situ measurements (n = 237). These maps suggest an aboveground woody carbon pool (AGC) in the dry tropics of 25.3 ±$$ \pm $$ 2.0 PgC, ~13.0% of global AGC. Net AGC has increased by 0.43 ±$$ \pm $$ 0.07 PgC yr−1, ~20.0% of the global net land sink. The overall net increase (0.43 PgC yr−1) is comprised of gross losses from deforestation and degradation (0.27 ±$$ \pm $$ 0.05 PgC yr−1) and gains due to densification and extensification of 0.59 ±$$ \pm $$ 0.1 PgC yr−1, with the balance accounted for by small changes (change < 20% of AGCD; 0.11 PgC yr−1). Losses are equally split between degradation and deforestation, while gains are divided roughly 2:1 between the densification of woody ecosystems and expansion into previously grass‐dominated areas. These new maps, created with a dry‐tropics‐specific EO method, highlight the importance of tropical dry forests and savannas in the global carbon cycle. The prominent role of degradation‐related losses suggests that climate change mitigation will need to focus much more on reducing losses from overharvesting than at present. The widespread increases in carbon density and the increase in tree biomass into open systems present major challenges for biodiversity conservation, restoration and livelihoods.
nfd62231b2efe: Climate change is widely expected to push many taxa beyond their biological limits, yet some populations persist in environments that routinely experience climatic extremes. This raises a fundamental question: does their thermal tolerance reflect species‐level thermal generalism (an evolved capacity to maintain performance across a broad thermal range) or population‐specific acclimation to local conditions (phenotypic plasticity)? Distinguishing between these alternatives is key for predicting whether tolerance to climatic extremes will generalise across species distributions or remain restricted to heat‐tolerant populations. To test these competing hypotheses, we quantified physiological performance (at cellular and organismal levels) in three economically important estuarine fish (Acanthopagrus australis, Sillago ciliata and Rhabdosargus sarba) collected from 20 sites across 15 estuaries along a ~1000‐km latitudinal gradient spanning their core and poleward range edges. Sites differed in thermal variability, including some that intermittently exceeded the severest end‐of‐century climate projections. We then experimentally exposed two of the fish species from low and high thermal variability sites to moderate (+2°C, 14 days) or extreme (+4°C, 7 days) simulated marine heatwave events, assessing 12 physiological and behavioural proxies. All three species collected in situ maintained comparable physiological performance across sites of contrasting thermal variability. Both experimental species, each collected from a single high‐ and low‐variability site, tolerated heatwave conditions regardless of thermal history or heatwave intensity, supporting species‐level thermal generalism rather than population‐specific acclimation. In the absence of heatwave conditions, S. ciliata from high‐variability sites also showed steeper allometric scaling and faster growth at 26 versus 24°C experimental control temperatures, suggesting this species may benefit from the warmer baseline temperatures projected under gradual climate change. Combined, our findings support thermal generalism as the primary driver of tolerance in estuarine fishes to climatic extremes, with important implications for the fisheries they support under climate change.
n6299c4a3aa98: Many species are responding to environmental change by shifting the timings of phenological events such as migration or reproduction. These shifts are typically reported as rates of change, which do not indicate when such shifts transcend their original states, nor consider whether species experience novel environmental conditions or phenological mismatch with other species at their phenological events. We present a new, generalizable approach to detect and contextualize shifts in phenological data regardless of taxonomic group or location by applying statistical and empirical Time of Emergence (ToE) metrics derived from climate science. Our approach conclusively identifies when species depart from their baseline phenological event timings and determines whether they experience novel environmental conditions or phenological mismatch with other species during their phenological event. In combination, these metrics detect emergence in timing, environment and community synchrony for species' phenological responses. We explore these metrics using simulations then apply them to a diverse set of example datasets (butterflies, marine plankton and cherry blossoms). We then develop community‐wide indicators of phenological emergence, environmental emergence and species mismatch, which can be applied to inform biodiversity policy at any scale and for any taxa. These methods are available via the phenometrics R package.
n23dbb4bb3a1f: Datasets derived from mixed‐template DNA amplification and sequencing (‘metabarcoding’) are common in environmental DNA (eDNA), microbiome or microbial ecology analyses. Such metabarcoding data have been broadly used to inform estimates of biodiversity, distribution and abundance across a wide range of species and habitats. Generally, data from metabarcoding consist of a table of read‐counts assigned to each of a set of taxa or sequence variants. As such, they appear to contain quantitative information about the environment under study, immediately eligible for traditional community ecology analyses. In fact, metabarcoding data are compositional, can be biased by variation in PCR amplification rates among taxa, and have other statistical attributes that are distinct from many other common ecological observations. The difficulty in understanding and accounting for the complexity of metabarcoding observations has hindered their ecological interpretation and limited their integration with other ecological data types. Here, we use both simulations and empirical observations to show that the variability among replicate metabarcoding observations is closely tied to the absolute quantities of DNA present in a sample. We then develop a general statistical model for estimating DNA abundance from metabarcoding observations using the relationship between mean and variance of metabarcoding reads. We demonstrate that the model can effectively estimate DNA abundances using simulations and from experimentally created DNA samples. The model can be applied to a single marker or to multiple markers simultaneously, allowing the direct integration of information from multiple genetic markers derived from a common biological sample. Estimates of absolute DNA abundance are the logical unit to connect DNA observations to organismal abundance or biomass. Our methods can be used to link together multiple types of DNA observations or to connect DNA observations with non‐genetic ecological methods for surveying ecosystems. However, important aspects of the ‘ecology of DNA’ remain unresolved and may limit our ability to link observed concentrations to organismal abundances in a general way.
nbf5db98f9e53: Tropical forest canopies host diverse tree and liana assemblages, yet key foliar and reproductive traits needed for taxonomic identification of canopy plants are often difficult to see from the forest floor, creating a bottleneck in inventories. We introduce a drone-based workflow that automatically acquires hundreds of close-up, ultra-high-resolution photographs (~0.4 mm pixel−1) of selected tree crowns per day, enabling efficient botanical and ecological studies of canopy plants (demo: https://youtu.be/80goMEifpc4). The approach leverages a compact DJI Mavic 3 Enterprise (M3E) with wide-angle and telephoto cameras to (i) generate a high-resolution digital surface model and orthomosaic via structure-from-motion photogrammetry and (ii) capture close-up photographs from ~6 m above the canopy at preplanned locations. Photographs are accurately (<13 cm error) geolocated with real-time kinematic (RTK) global navigation satellite system to support spatial co-registration with photogrammetric products. In field deployments, we acquired close-up photographs for up to ~300 selected canopy trees per day and maintained RTK corrections over operational distances up to ~3 km, illustrating the potential of the method for plot- to landscape-scale studies. The level of visual detail in the close-up photographs of canopy crowns was sufficient to support expert identification in a majority of cases in our tropical forest study sites despite their high taxonomic diversity. Although developed for tropical trees and lianas, the workflow is applicable to other forest and vegetation types for botanical, phenological and ecological applications. We outline strengths and limitations of the workflow to guide use and also provide harpia , an open-source Python library to program automatic close-up missions with the M3E (code: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22116831). Resumen El dosel de los bosques tropicales alberga diversas comunidades de árboles y lianas. Sin embargo, las características foliares y reproductivas clave necesarias para la identificación taxonómica de las especies del dosel suelen ser difíciles de observar desde el suelo del bosque, lo que limita el progreso en los inventarios. Presentamos un flujo de trabajo basado en drones que adquiere automáticamente cientos de fotografías de primer plano de ultra alta resolución (~0,4 mm píxel−1) de copas de árboles seleccionadas por día, agilizando los estudios botánicos y ecológicos de las especies del dosel (demostración: https://youtu.be/80goMEifpc4). Utilizamos un dron DJI Mavic 3 Enterprise (M3E) compacto, equipado con cámaras gran angular y teleobjetivo, para (i) generar un modelo digital de superficie y un ortomosaico de alta resolución mediante fotogrametría de estructura a partir del movimiento (structure-from-motion) y (ii) capturar fotografías de primer plano desde ~6 m sobre el dosel en ubicaciones planificadas previamente. Las fotografías se georreferencian con precisión (error <13 cm) mediante un sistema global de navegación por satélite (GNSS) con posicionamiento cinemático en tiempo real (RTK), facilitando su corregistro espacial con los productos fotogramétricos. En campañas de campo, adquirimos fotografías de primer plano de hasta ~300 árboles de dosel diarios y mantuvimos correcciones RTK a distancias operativas de hasta ~3 km, lo que evidencia el potencial del método para estudios desde nivel de parcela hasta paisaje. La alta resolución de las fotografías permitió la identificación taxonómica por expertos en la mayoría de los casos, aun en ecosistemas de bosque tropical con elevada diversidad taxonómica. Aunque se desarrolló para árboles y lianas tropicales, el flujo de trabajo es aplicable a otros tipos de bosques y vegetación con fines botánicos, fenológicos y ecológicos.…
n228d8356b644: Individual‐tree segmentation from three‐dimensional forest point clouds underpins forest inventory, biomass estimation and ecosystem monitoring, but remains challenging in structurally complex stands, where vertical heterogeneity and point‐density degradation weaken the robustness of centre‐offset‐based instance grouping. We present TreeSegAgent, an extensible framework for forest point‐cloud analysis, whose core segmentation component is a multi‐anchor framework for tree segmentation (MA‐TreeSeg). MA‐TreeSeg stabilizes instance formation through two modules. First, a multi‐anchor (three‐vertical‐anchor) structural grouping module within an enhanced PointGroup‐style instance segmentation network, explicitly encoding tree vertical structure to improve grouping stability under sparse canopy conditions and to better recover low‐stature and understory trees. Second, we incorporate segment anything model (SAM)‐driven trunk constraint module. SAM is applied on two‐dimensional projections to identify trunk regions and generate trunk candidates, which are then employed as spatial hard constraints to regularize centre‐offset predictions and suppress clustering drift under canopy overlap. To support reproducible ecological workflow, TreeSegAgent further provides a task‐driven agent for automated, specification‐driven orchestration of common point‐cloud operations (e.g. instance segmentation, DEM generation and height‐based filtering) across datasets. Across multiple forest point‐cloud benchmarks, our method yields more spatially coherent individual‐tree instances and improved robustness to density variation, offering an extensible solution for large‐scale forest point‐cloud analysis.
n13a59ef7daa3: Photopigments, formed by an opsin protein bound to a light‐sensitive chromophore, underlie vertebrate vision. Long‐wavelength–sensitive (LWS) opsins mediate red‐light detection, and most teleosts retain a single functional LWS1. A shorter‐shifted green‐sensitive paralog (LWS2) is found only in a few lineages. By mining teleost genomes and sequencing retinal transcriptomes, we identify elopomorphs as an additional lineage retaining LWS2 (alongside characins and osteoglossomorphs). Surprisingly, we reveal a previously overlooked, shorter‐shifted paralog, LWS3, restricted to gobies (Percomorpha) and arising from an ancestral duplication either in the teleost or in the percomorph ancestor. Structural modelling of twelve LWS opsins reveals convergent evolution at four key amino acid sites (214, 259, 261, 269) in the retinal‐binding pocket, indicating convergent substitutions in human MWS (an old‐world primate‐specific duplicate of the vertebrate LWS1), teleost LWS2, and goby LWS3 relative to red‐sensitive counterparts, consistent with repeated spectral shifts towards greener wavelengths. In several lineages, including characins, mormyrids, gobies, and primates, these shorter‐shifted LWS opsins have at least partially replaced the canonical green‐sensitive RH2‐based visual pigment. Retinal transcriptomes revealed variable lws3 expression across adult gobies, either complementing lws1 in most species, or dominating the visual opsin expression profile as in the sicydiines. In situ hybridisation in the whitebarred goby (Amblygobius phalaena; Valenciennes, 1837) showed that lws1 and lws3 are expressed in separate double‐cone members, analogous to rh2 expression in other fish species. Together, these results show that repeated convergence towards shorter LWS sensitivity in vertebrate evolution involves coordinated changes at the molecular, regulatory, and functional levels, providing a striking example of multilevel sensory adaptation.
nf47d45fbe9fa: Grassland CH4 sink stability is governed by divergent pathways under distinct drought regimes. While intense drought triggers transient inhibition via legacy effects on belowground productivity (BNPPlag), chronic drought and reduced rainfall frequency exert persistent suppression through coupled biotic‐abiotic shifts. Notably, Artemisia frigida expansion stimulates biogenic methane emissions, significantly offsetting soil CH4 oxidation. This suppression is reinforced by diminished arbuscular mycorrhizal fungal (AMF) abundance and altered nutrient availability, whereas nitrogen addition acts as a functional buffer under specific scenarios. Summary Drought and nitrogen (N) deposition alter greenhouse gas fluxes, but how distinct drought scenarios interact with N enrichment to regulate the methane (CH4) sink remains poorly understood. We conducted a 4‐yr field experiment in a temperate steppe to examine CH4 fluxes under three drought regimes – early‐season intense drought (ID), mid‐season chronic drought (CD), and mid‐season reduced rainfall frequency (RF) – and N addition. CH4 uptake and its driving mechanisms were assessed through field measurements and structural equation modeling, focusing on the interplay between soil physicochemical properties, microbial abundance, and plant‐mediated emissions. All drought treatments reduced the CH4 sink with divergent temporal dynamics; reduced RF caused the most persistent reduction, while N addition alleviated the inhibitory effects of CD. These shifts were driven by distinct mechanisms: ID acted via lowering previous‐year belowground net primary productivity and increasing dissolved organic N, CD functioned through increased Artemisia frigida cover and reduced arbuscular mycorrhizal fungal abundance, and RF suppressed uptake via the morphological expansion of A. frigida. We conclude that CH4 sink stability is highly sensitive to drought regime, and that the morphological expansion of specific plants such as A. frigida may partially offset the soil CH4 sink.
ne55d8e019a9a: Representative South African Helichrysum species illustrating variation in capitulum size. Summary Gynomonoecy has evolved repeatedly in Asteraceae, suggesting selective advantages for species whose capitula combine pistillate and bisexual flowers. Theories invoking conspicuous peripheral flowers and achene heteromorphism do not account for gynomonoecy in the southern African‐centred genus Helichrysum, which lacks both these features. We investigated whether gynomonoecy is associated with changes in capitulum architecture in South African Helichrysum, focusing on flower packing density and achene size. We compared flower packing density and achene size between hermaphroditic and gynomonoecious Helichrysum species using phylogenetic generalised least squares and reconstructed ancestral sexual systems using a well‐sampled, time‐calibrated phylogeny. Gynomonoecious species produced nearly twice as many flowers per unit receptacle area as hermaphroditic species and had subtly but significantly smaller achenes. Ancestral‐state reconstruction strongly supported hermaphroditism as ancestral, with gynomonoecy originating independently 18 times. Our results provide the first phylogenetically informed evidence within a single Asteraceae genus that shifts to gynomonoecy correlate with shifts in capitulum architecture. The association between gynomonoecy, denser flower packing, and reduced achene size is consistent with the hypothesis that accentuated resource gradients within capitula and priority access to resources by first‐maturing peripheral flowers may have favoured the evolution of gynomonoecy.
n7c0c32db6080: Reproductive dynamics strongly influence genetic diversity and population structure, with important implications for ecological interactions and evolutionary trajectories. However, our understanding of plant reproductive dynamics remains limited due to the scarcity of long-term studies. Here, we propose a conceptual and methodological framework for tracking plant reproductive dynamics over long timescales using pollen, plant spore, and seed records preserved in sedimentary archives. The analysis of counts, morphology, and DNA from fossil propagules enables reconstruction of reproductive patterns over centennial to million-year timescales. When integrated with other palaeoproxies, these records provide insights into environmental drivers and eco-evolutionary consequences of reproductive dynamics. The proposed framework opens new avenues for optimising conservation strategies, safeguarding key ecological functions, and improving predictions of future biotic responses.
n85ec88ac17db: Participation in authentic research projects benefits both teachers and students by linking hands‐on field work with experimental biology and quantitative analysis. Plant ecological genetics is especially well suited for classroom integration, but accessible, classroom‐ready outlines are scarce. Arabidopsis thaliana—a wild species in urban environments with a well‐characterized genome and extensive educational resources—provides an ideal model. Here we present a comprehensive, easy‐to‐implement pipeline for secondary‐school–level research‐oriented projects in plant ecological genetics using A. thaliana. The report includes (i) a step‐by‐step experimental workflow for field sampling, phenotypic scoring, and PCR‐sequencing‐based genotyping assays for environment‐sensitive allele monitoring; (ii) classroom‐adapted protocols and quality‐control checks; (iii) background material and a list of concrete, testable research questions; and (iv) downloadable real datasets and analysis templates for guided interpretation. We demonstrate feasibility with pilot field‐survey data from urban school neighborhoods and report outcomes that validate the approach as a proof of concept. Students can learn species identification, formulate hypotheses about ecological adaptation, perform standardized data collection, and apply elementary genetic and statistical analyses—thereby gaining practical laboratory skills and improved scientific literacy. The methods are adaptable to different time frames and resource levels and can be scaled into broader citizen‐science initiatives, allowing classroom findings to contribute meaningfully to ecological genetics research. This project therefore provides a practical bridge between secondary education and place‐based research, fostering engagement with contemporary questions in ecology and evolution.
n4b2f1cd24732: Dietary knowledge of migratory birds along their migration routes is fundamental for understanding ecological and evolutionary aspects of bird migration, how migrants select and repeatedly use specific non‐breeding areas, accumulate fuel for migration and breeding, and assess carrying capacity at key sites in the migratory network. Local changes in food availability and foraging habitat have been shown to contribute to population declines in migratory shorebirds. Nevertheless, the diet of many migratory bird populations remains unknown at key migratory sites. We address this knowledge gap for Black‐tailed Godwits (Limosa limosa) by exploring their diet in the Ganges–Brahmaputra–Meghna delta in the Bay of Bengal, a key non‐breeding site overlapping the Central Asian and East Asian–Australasian flyways. We assessed how benthic prey availability changed during their non‐breeding period based on 600 mud samples collected from 120 foraging locations between October 2018 and March 2019. In mid‐January 2019, we determined godwit diets by analyzing undigested remains of 15 feces and 15 pellets collected from roosting areas, and compared dietary composition with benthic prey availability from samples collected concurrently. Polychaetes and oligochaetes were the most abundant benthic groups in the mud, but we did not find them in the droppings. We observed intra‐seasonal changes in abundance and body size of bivalvia, decapoda, and gastropoda, which were the main animal foods found in droppings and mud samples, and were positively selected by godwits based on availability compared to other benthic prey. We also found plant materials, rice kernels, and rhizomes of Porteresia coarctata, in one‐third of the droppings. This finding extends previous evidence of godwits' herbivory in the East‐Atlantic flyway to Asian flyways. Scaling up our efforts to systematic monitoring could help address conservation questions, such as the impact of shellfish harvesting on the carrying capacity of the world's largest river delta for shorebirds.
nd1f3334a6c18: Anthropogenic changes are driving global shifts in species distributions. Two highly divergent bird species, the green jay (Cyanocorax yncas) and the blue jay (Cyanocitta cristata), recently hybridized in Texas following range expansions. While the southwestern spread of the blue jay has been attributed to suburban bird‐feeding, the cause of the green jay's > 2° northward expansion over the last 70 years is less clear. Climate change has been proposed as a driver, but concurrent changes in habitat and resource availability—including widespread supplemental feeding of deer—complicate interpretation. We combine ornithological records, eBird observations, climate data, and economic data to investigate the progression of the green jay's range expansion in relation to climate and supplemental feeding. The first records of resident green jays north of southernmost Texas occurred in the 1960s. Sustained northward expansion was detectable from 1980 to 2021 and coincided with reduced severe freeze frequency from 1982 to 1996. Severe winters occurred alongside a reduced probability of green jay detections in newly occupied locations. However, range expansion increased during the period with the coldest average winter in the 95‐year climate record and coincided with growing supplemental feeding. We suggest that winter food supply on widespread hunting ranches and habitat loss drove initial northward colonization by green jays. Subsequent warming may have then relaxed climatic constraints once this novel resource became widespread. This potential interaction between novel resources and climate change highlights that different anthropogenic mechanisms may work together to alter species distributions.
nbf55176cf206: Parasitoid wasps are important regulators of their hosts and highly relevant for the resilience of terrestrial ecosystems. However, data on parasitoid‐host interactions are scarce and missing for many parasitoid species as parasitoids are mostly collected as adults without host association and rearing of parasitoids from their hosts can be difficult. Molecular methods can thus help to circumvent this bottleneck. We here present cuticular barcoding, a novel non‐destructive molecular approach to identify parasitoid‐host associations from adult parasitoid wasps. We tested our approach by rearing the parasitoid wasp Lariophagus distinguendus on two beetle species, and washing off remnant host DNA from the wasp cuticle to detect the host species using DNA barcoding. Our results showed a success rate of 49%, detecting the host species in 35 out of 72 samples. Samples containing pooled wasp specimens performed equally well as single wasp specimens, which indicates that single field‐collected wasps are sufficient to identify host associations. Hosts could be detected in wasps that were fixated either through freezing or ethanol, which also supports the application of this method in the field. The primers Jerry/Pat targeting the mitochondrial COI gene performed better than the universal primers LCO/HCO, indicating that more studies testing universal primers are needed to establish this method. This non‐destructive method allows to preserve the sampled wasp as a physical voucher for subsequent morphological identification which will be essential for its usage in situ. Our study presents a novel method that enables detection of parasitoid‐host interactions, and holds significant potential for conservation ecologists, pest managers and evolutionary biologists.
n4ff9e4ae2f32: Vertebrate mitochondrial protein‐coding genes follow a different genetic code, in which TGA encodes tryptophan and a large number of genes terminate with incomplete stop codons completed post‐transcriptionally via polyadenylation. These features are often mishandled when coding sequences (CDS) downloaded from public databases are processed with standard tools, resulting in errors in downstream codon usage and evolution. Here we present FishMitoCleaner, a Python command line tool automating quality control and normalisation of fish mitochondrial CDS sequences in five steps: character validation, internal stop codon scanning, terminal TGA detection, stop codon processing and length normalisation. FishMitoCleaner cleaned 97.6% of input sequences in 22 fish species representing 7 orders and all 13 mitochondrial protein coding genes. Statistical comparison of RSCU values confirmed no bias in codon usage analysis (Welch's t‐test, all p > 0.05). FishMitoCleaner is a Python command that allows researchers in aquatic biology and fisheries science to perform rigorous and reproducible CDS quality control in a single command, and clean sequences ready to be analysed in downstream analyses. FishMitoCleaner is also applicable to mitochondrial CDS data from other vertebrate taxa.
ne74d2a6bb75d: Species that span heterogenous environments often exhibit local adaptation despite gene flow among populations. In such cases, the maintenance of local adaptation is controlled by several factors, including the strength of selection, migration, assortative mating, and genomic architecture. The song sparrow (Melospiza melodia) is a widespread songbird with diverse subspecies, including the coastally adapted Atlantic song sparrow (M. m. atlantica). Despite extensive gene flow with a generalist subspecies, Atlantic song sparrow populations have been found to maintain their coastally adaptive phenotypes. We produced a new chromosome‐level reference assembly for the species and whole‐genome data to explore the genomic architecture of divergence with gene flow and the genetic basis of adaptation in this subspecies. Adaptation in the Atlantic song sparrow has a polygenic basis, with loci under divergent selection scattered throughout the genome rather than concentrated in low‐recombination linkage blocks. Signatures of fine‐scale population structure, limited genomic differentiation, and divergent selection on a small set of genes suggest a role for natural selection in maintaining this subspecies boundary. Our findings highlight the complex interplay among selection, gene flow, and recombination in shaping adaptation with gene flow and provide insights into the genomic architecture of ecological divergence within a widespread, morphologically diverse species.
n3fd7e86f7f93: Plant communities are shaped by interactions among plants and soil legacies. Plant–soil feedbacks (PSF) may alter invasion dynamics and change plant community species composition. There have been field observations of the invasive annual grass, Ventenata dubia, replacing another invasive annual grass, Bromus tectorum, though previous work has not found evidence of competition that would support these shifts. The goal of this study was to determine if PSF via soil legacies and competition are present between co‐occurring invasive annual grasses B. tectorum and V. dubia, and if so, quantify their effects on interactions with these species. We measured aboveground per capita biomass of these species grown in biculture with three field soils (neutral, B. tectorum, V. dubia) over two experimental Phases in a greenhouse. We evaluated biomass in Phase 1 with field‐conditioned soil, and Phase 2 in soil conditioned from Phase 1. We used generalized linear mixed models to determine the effect of soil origin and plant density on biomass, and non‐linear analysis to quantify competition regression coefficients. The linear analysis showed intraspecific competition negatively impacted both species in both Phases, but by Phase 2 interspecific competition was weakened in conspecific soil, suggesting positive PSF. Intraspecific competition coefficients were always greater than interspecific coefficients from the non‐linear analysis across soil origins. These results are suggestive of a positive PSF which may alter the strength of competition between these species in a biculture. Understanding how PSF influences interactions between these species provides insight into how their invasion dynamics may change over time.
nf6f6dea7159a: Wings play a central role in shaping dispersal, behavior, and ecological specialization of insects. In social insects, distinct castes with specialized morphologies arise from a shared genome, raising the question of how divergence of traits, such as wings, occurs despite genetic constraints. We investigated genetic constraints and sources of variation in wing shape in the Eastern yellowjacket wasp (Vespula maculifrons), combining geometric morphometrics and quantitative genetic analyses across queens, workers, and males. Landmark‐based Procrustes analyses revealed strong divergence in mean wing shape among castes. Males showed greater wing‐shape variation than queens and workers, consistent with weaker stabilizing selection. Allometric analyses revealed that individual‐level size‐shape relationships are weak across all castes, with no caste showing consistent significant allometry across colonies, indicating that size‐related developmental programs do not strongly couple wing shape to body size. Wing shape also varied significantly among colonies, revealing a substantial colony‐level component of wing‐shape variation that may reflect shared environmental, genetic, and socially mediated developmental influences. Additionally, we found that queens and workers from different patrilineal subfamilies differed in wing shape, demonstrating substantial heritable contributions. Our analyses also revealed limited genetic correlations between worker and queen wing shape components, suggesting that shared genetic architecture would not strongly constrain independent caste evolution of wing morphology. Together, these results show that variation in wing shape in V. maculifrons is shaped by a balance of genetic diversity generated by polyandry, colony‐level environmental variation, including environmental and genetic influences, and caste‐specific selective pressures associated with division of labor. Thus, caste‐specialized wing morphology can evolve in insect societies despite a shared genome and genetic constraints.
n7bc72ac7ac26: Drawing on two decades of research in East Greenland, this study shows that little auks, key seabird indicators of Arctic ecosystem health, can adapt to rapid environmental change through behavioural flexibility. However, increasing storms and mercury pollution are pushing resilience to its limits, providing an early warning of broader Arctic disruption. Abstract Long‐term ecological studies testing global change impacts are rare yet essential in the Arctic, a region warming nearly four times faster than the global average. These rapid environmental changes reshape ecosystem functioning across the pan‐Arctic and affect the livelihoods of local communities. Seabirds are widely recognised indicators of environmental change. Identifying species‐specific critical constraints is therefore essential for detecting early warning signals of population decline and ecosystem reorganisation. Little auks (Alle alle), the most abundant Arctic seabirds, are key ecosystem engineers shaping coastal environments through for example food‐web interactions and guano deposition. We present a 20‐year study (2005–2024) of an East Greenland little auk population, combining long‐term demographic monitoring with behavioural, physiological and ecotoxicological data. We quantified fitness‐related traits (adult body condition, overwinter survival and chick growth) alongside potential constraints, including parental foraging effort, trophic ecology, winter distribution, and mercury contamination in adults, eggs and chicks. Over the study period, climate‐driven ocean warming, sea‐ice decline, altered zooplankton communities, and increasing mercury exposure reshaped environmental conditions. Faced with these changes, little auks exhibited marked behavioural and dietary plasticity, allowing them to maintain relatively stable fitness metrics in most years. However, sustained monitoring revealed key constraints that undermine this apparent resilience: (a) Elevated mercury burdens may reduce aerobic diving capacity and thermal tolerance in adults and were associated with reduced reproductive performance. (b) Chick growth was strongly impaired during years with increased summer storm activity, which disrupted adult foraging trips and provisioning rates. Winter storms are also likely to negatively affect adult overwinter survival. Together, these findings show that little auks can partially buffer rapid Arctic change through behavioural flexibility, but multiple interacting climatic and contaminant stressors impose increasing, possibly cumulative constraints on performance. Identifying such critical constraints is crucial for understanding the limits of resilience in wild populations and for improving predictions of ecosystem responses to ongoing climate change.
nb25bd11d1684: Conceptual framework for family‐level classification. Summary Plant family names are routinely used to structure comparative analyses, trait databases, floras, conservation assessments, and teaching. Yet, these names are not neutral labels: changing family boundaries changes the units across which biological patterns are compared, summarized, and interpreted. Modern phylogenetic inference resolves evolutionary relationships with increasing confidence, but it does not by itself determine which monophyletic groups should be recognized as families. We argue that this choice should be guided not only by monophyly, but also by diagnosability, biological interpretability, stability, and practical utility. Recent debates around large‐scale consensus classifications show why these criteria must be explicit. Recognizing classification as shared scientific infrastructure means that family delimitation matters not only to systematists, but to all plant scientists who rely on taxonomic units to formulate questions and communicate results.
nb782d3fae29d: Timeline of key eco‐evolutionary outcomes arising from belowground allocation of recent plant photosynthate from shoots. Summary Plants rapidly allocate carbon from photosynthesis belowground via root exudates and root‐associated microorganisms. Here we synthesise recent evidence of our understanding of the consequences of this ‘fast’ pathway of recent photosynthate flux for major ecological and evolutionary processes. This rapid input of plant‐derived carbon to soils shapes food webs and drives processes including soil CO2 efflux, nutrient cycling, plant community dynamics, stability of symbioses and evolution of contrasting modes of nutrition, such as parasitism and mycoheterotrophy. We also highlight how seasonality and anthropogenic and natural perturbations likely determine the magnitude and dynamics of this fast pathway across major vegetation types, but these factors remain understudied. Further gaps in understanding include demonstrating causal links between photosynthate flow and key biogeochemical cycling processes and the capture of photosynthate by co‐occurring root‐associated microorganisms.
nfe7ae5aff148: Working model illustrating the CDK‐MAP65‐microtubule module mediating salt stress adaptation in Arabidopsis. Summary Plants possess sophisticated regulatory mechanisms to balance growth and stress responses. Cyclin‐dependent kinases (CDKs) are established regulators of cell division and endoreduplication, yet their roles in abiotic stress responses remain poorly understood. Here, using reverse genetics, biochemical, and cell biological approaches, we show that Arabidopsis (Arabidopsis thaliana) CDKB1s contribute to salt stress adaptation through a mechanism involving the phosphorylation of MAP65‐1 and MAP65‐2, two microtubule‐associated proteins essential for cytoskeleton dynamics under salt stress. Loss of CDKB1 function enhances salt tolerance, accompanied by attenuated plasma membrane depolarization and reactive oxygen species accumulation. In vitro phosphorylation assays demonstrate that CDKB1;1 directly phosphorylates MAP65‐1 at Ser‐503. Genetic analyses indicate that phospho‐dead MAP65 variants confer enhanced salt tolerance, whereas phosphomimetic variants compromise tolerance even in the cdkb1;1 1;2 background, supporting a critical role for MAP65 phosphorylation status at these sites in salt stress adaptation. We further found that CDKA;1 can similarly interact with and phosphorylate MAP65‐1, suggesting a potential parallel role for CDKA;1 in this process. Collectively, our findings identify a regulatory module involving CDKs, MAP65, and microtubules that links cell cycle kinases and cytoskeleton dynamics with plant salt stress adaptation.
n6630d64ba919: Phloem‐specific silencing of PIN3 impairs polar auxin transport and auxin response in Populus tomentosa. Summary Auxin is a central regulator of tree secondary growth and forms maxima in the vascular cambium, yet how these maxima are established remains elusive. Here, we functionally characterized two redundant PIN‐FORMED 3 (PIN3) paralogs from Populus tomentosa to define their roles in secondary growth and gravity‐induced tension wood (TW) formation. We employed fluorescent reporter lines, clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats‐generated knockout mutants, phloem‐specific RNA interference transgenic plants and isotopic auxin transport assays to dissect PIN3 functions during secondary growth of poplar stems. Loss of function of PIN3 paralogs severely compromises cambial proliferation, secondary xylem differentiation and TW development. PIN3 proteins display cell‐type‐specific polar localization with basal polarity in phloem cells and outer lateral polarity in endodermal cells. Phloem‐expressed PIN3 facilitates basipetal auxin transport and is required for cambial auxin response. Upon gravistimulation, endodermal PIN3 repolarizes along the gravity vector, correlating with TW formation. Our findings identify a cell‐type‐specific, PIN3‐mediated auxin transport mechanism that contributes to auxin‐driven secondary growth of tree stems.
n063a51f018ad: Community trait variation (a), community‐weighted trait overlap (b), intraspecific trait variation (ITV, c), and its relative contribution to community trait variation (rITV, d) for all the four examined traits under different treatments (mean ± SE, n = 12). Summary Trait‐based studies on community assembly under environmental change often overlook intraspecific trait variation (ITV), despite its considerable role in modulating community dynamics, which may largely mislead the inference of community assembly. Under simulated extreme droughts in a temperate steppe, we integrated ITV and interspecific trait variation for four key traits, plant height (Height), specific leaf area (SLA), leaf dry matter content (LDMC), and leaf thickness (LT), to examine how drought alters functional niche structure and underlying processes. Drought shifted communities toward conservative resource‐use strategies, reduced community variation in LT, and interspecific trait overlap in terms of SLA, LDMC, LT, and the multivariate trait space, whereas community‐level ITV remained stable across all traits. These changes were driven primarily by diversity loss and increases in the dominance of fewer species, with negligible effects of intraspecific trait plasticity or species turnover. Communities with fewer but more dominant species exhibited smaller trait overlap. Our findings advance our understanding of the paradigm of trait convergence under environmental filtering. Drought‐induced diversity loss amplifies functional niche differentiation, underscoring the critical role of species reorganization through dominance shifts, with little evidence for intraspecific trait plasticity in mediating community assembly under climate extremes.
nadba95464f6d: Precise editing of upstream open reading frames enabled in situ fine-tuning of gene expression in allohexaploid wheat, thereby enhancing abiotic stress tolerance without growth penalties. Summary Developing climate-resilient crops is critical for ensuring global food security, yet agricultural productivity is frequently constrained by the trade-off between stress tolerance and growth. This challenge is particularly acute in allohexaploid wheat, a staple crop susceptible to abiotic stresses, underscoring the demand for precise gene regulation. Here, we established a simple, efficient, and transgene-free method for regulating gene expression in allohexaploid wheat by disrupting or creating de novo upstream open reading frames (uORFs) via genome editing. Using ribosome profiling, we identified 1199 actively translated uORFs across the wheat genome and developed a dual-luciferase screening pipeline to pinpoint potent translational repressors of positive regulators of abiotic stress. CRISPR/Cas9-mediated disruption of the uORFs in TaCIPK14 and TaGGP1 elevated downstream protein accumulation, thereby enhancing drought, cold, and salt tolerance of plants. Furthermore, base editing was employed to generate de novo uORFs in TaMADS26, effectively downregulating gene expression and improving drought resilience. Notably, both the transgene-free uorf TaGGP1-ACG and uORFTaMADS26 mutants conferred pronounced yield advantages under drought conditions without incurring growth penalties under well-watered conditions. This study provides a predictable and precise way for modulating gene expression, enabling the coordinated improvement of stress resilience and agronomic performance in wheat.
n4fc656dd75e7: miR160 links salicylic acid, auxin, and redox signaling with the growth–defense trade‐off in the potato hypersensitive response to potato virus Y. Summary Hypersensitive response (HR) is an effector‐triggered immune response leading to pathogen restriction and local cell death. Small RNAs (sRNAs), mediating RNA silencing, have a well‐established role in antiviral immunity; however, their role in HR has not been addressed to date. We applied a spatially resolved sRNA‐omics approach to uncover changes at the sRNA level and the dynamics of sRNA–gene regulatory networks in potato (Solanum tuberosum L.) HR to potato virus Y (PVY). We show that miR160 is repressed in cells adjacent to HR lesions in the resistant cultivar, but not in PVY‐sensitive, salicylic acid (SA)‐depleted plants. Beyond its canonical regulation of StARF10 and StARF17, miR160 controls a broader regulatory network spanning auxin signaling, cell‐wall remodeling, redox homeostasis, and tuberization. Elevated miR160 levels promote susceptibility‐associated traits, reduce thermotolerance, and suppress genes strongly activated in HR. Mechanistically, we identify a novel miR160–StARF10/StARF17–StPRX28 module that links miR160 repression to the induction of a Class III apoplastic peroxidase in HR, with SA acting upstream. Together, these findings establish miR160 as an important regulatory node that connects SA–auxin–redox signaling pathways and tunes development, defense, and heat resilience, and highlight miR160 as a promising target for fine‐tuning tolerance to multiple stresses with minimal yield loss.
n9b6adaf7e491: The Chinese mitten crab (Eriocheir sinensis), native to China and the Korean Peninsula, has established invasive populations with substantial ecological and economic impacts in Europe and North America. Anticipating changes in its potential distribution is important for invasion‐risk screening and estuarine management. We developed a global species distribution model (G‐SDM) and regional models for the native range, Europe, and North America, each comprising terrestrial and nearshore brackish‐water components. Future suitability was projected under SSP126, SSP245, and SSP585. Terrestrial PCA‐env analyses assessed changes in projected suitable environmental space, whereas MESS and MoD diagnosed environmental novelty and extrapolation uncertainty. Terrestrial suitability was mainly associated with annual mean temperature, annual precipitation, and distance to the coastline, whereas nearshore suitability was mainly associated with water depth, chlorophyll concentration, and sea‐surface temperature, although the ranking of predictor importance differed among regions. Predicted‐suitable environments in Europe and North America extended to lower annual and wettest‐quarter temperatures than those in the native range. Under future scenarios, projected suitability was generally redistributed towards higher latitudes, particularly under SSP585. Terrestrial suitability showed more pronounced spatial redistribution than nearshore suitability in several regions, and the two components were not always geographically aligned. Terrestrial PCA‐env analyses indicated greater retention of suitable environmental space in Europe but increasing unfilling in the native range and North America. MESS analysis further identified environmental novelty and extrapolation uncertainty in some future suitable areas. These findings provide a scientific basis for early prevention, targeted monitoring, field validation, and estuarine management.
nb52d3912f242: Understanding how large herbivores adjust their movement patterns in response to seasonal environmental variation is important for wildlife management. We investigated how sympatric African herbivores with contrasting body size, digestive systems and forage specialisation adjust their movement across seasons and the diel cycle. Using high‐resolution GPS data from 16 plains zebra (Equus quagga; hindgut fermenter) and 8 tsessebe (Damaliscus lunatus; ruminant) between 2014 and 2016 in the Okavango Delta, Botswana, we quantified 24 h range size, 24 h displacement distance, as well as displacement distance and tortuosity across 4 h time blocks, and evaluated these movements in response to season, maximum daily air temperature and vegetation greenness. Zebra occupied 24 h ranges double that of tsessebe during the rainy and early flood seasons, but 24 h range size converged during the late flood season. Zebra travelled twice the distance of tsessebe over 24 h during the early flood season, whereas travelling distances were similar during the rainy and late flood seasons. At finer temporal scales, both species showed pronounced but seasonally variable diel movement patterns. Movement paths were generally less tortuous in zebra than tsessebe, although interspecific differences diminished during the late flood season and midday. Movement patterns also changed with environmental conditions: increasing maximum daily air temperature was associated with a stronger reduction in movement in zebra than in tsessebe, whereas increasing vegetation productivity was associated with larger 24 h ranges and increased tortuosity, with the latter response stronger in zebra. Overall, our findings demonstrate that movement differences between zebra and tsessebe are strongly context‐dependent rather than constant across seasons. Movement convergence during the late flood season suggests that seasonal conditions can reduce otherwise pronounced interspecific differences in movement patterns. These findings improve our understanding of large herbivores' responses to seasonal environmental variation and may help predict species‐specific responses to future climate change.
nf3df5ca53c5a: Dung beetle density and sex ratio play a significant role in intraspecific competition, and reproductive success depends on the beetle's maturity. We examined the impact of increasing density in small groups on dung burial and brood production using mature first‐generation individuals of two dung beetle species (Onthophagus binodis and Digitonthophagus gazella) by manipulating the number of males and females in a dung pat. Beetles were reared under controlled laboratory conditions and provided with cattle dung, which was collected from pastureland. Weekly dung burial was calculated by measuring the residual dung organic matter content. The number of broods produced per dung pat, broods' dry weight, and their size were recorded. In both species, treatments with intermediate numbers of male and female beetles produced more broods than solitary beetles. On the other hand, treatments with moderate to high numbers of male and female beetles buried more dung than individual females. At higher‐density treatments, brood size and brood dry weight declined, suggesting shifts in reproductive allocation under increasing intraspecific interactions. The two species showed very similar patterns, although O. binodis produced more broods while D. gazella buried more dung. We also observed a positive relationship between brood dry weight and brood size in both species. Overall, the results indicate that the combined effects of beetle density and sex ratio influenced reproductive investment and dung burial under controlled laboratory conditions. Further field studies are needed to determine whether similar patterns occur under higher density and natural ecological conditions.
n33067f7372a8: Dothistroma needle blight (DNB), caused by Dothistroma septosporum, is a globally important disease of pines, yet its ecological role within native host systems remains incompletely understood. We combined species‐specific quantitative PCR (qPCR) with ITS2 metabarcoding to investigate the occurrence of D. septosporum and associated needle mycobiomes of Pinus sylvestris in natural stands in Slovakia with a pooled non‐natural positive‐reference group included for comparison. D. septosporum was detected in the Vernár natural stand (11 of 16 samples), where visible DNB symptoms were also observed, and in all samples of the non‐natural positive‐reference group (15 of 15 samples). The pathogen was not detected in the other three sampled natural stands. Fungal community analyzes revealed significant differences in community composition among sample groups, while alpha diversity patterns showed comparatively minor variation. The most abundant genus across all sites was Lophodermium, whereas Dothistroma was highly abundant only in the non‐natural positive‐reference group. Co‐occurrence network analysis indicated that fungal communities were dominated by positive associations; however, patterns involving Dothistroma primarily reflected the positive‐reference group, where the pathogen was highly abundant. Our results suggest that D. septosporum is not a consistently detectable component of needle mycobiomes in native P. sylvestris stands in Slovakia and that its high abundance in the non‐natural positive‐reference group was associated with a distinct fungal community composition.
n64ae89ba6494: Reef‐building corals are key contributors in marine ecosystems, from warm, shallow reefs to cold, deep‐water habitats worldwide. Desmophyllym pertusum (Linnaeus, 1758) is one of the most important habitat‐forming cold‐water corals and has long been considered a cosmopolitan species. Yet phylogenetic relationships within the genus, as well as its relatedness to the synonymized genus Lophelia (Milne Edwards & Haime, 1849), remain poorly understood and debated. Here, we use nuclear ultraconserved elements and exons, complete mitochondrial genomes, and single nucleotide polymorphism data to show that populations of D. pertusum in the eastern and central North Pacific Ocean are genetically differentiated from those in the western and eastern Atlantic Ocean. Our results support the previously proposed synonymy of genera Lophelia and Desmophyllum (Ehrenberg, 1834). Morphological features of specimens from the Pacific Ocean, particularly budding pattern and corallite size, match those of the previously synonymized D. californicum comb. nov., which we therefore reinstate. We also incorporated solitary Desmophyllum spp. lineages into phylogenomic analyses, including a multispecies coalescence model. Taken together, these integrative taxonomic results indicate the presence of multiple Desmophyllum species beyond those currently recognized as valid. Future studies could incorporate phylogenomic approaches to better delimit species boundaries and avoid grouping distinct coral species.
n5de6e7d30cc1: Grazing is a key driver of structural and functional changes in desert steppe ecosystems. Soil nutrients are essential for plant growth, and grazing can alter soil nutrient availability through herbivory and trampling, which, in turn, may affect plant communities. However, the responses of plant communities and their functional groups to soil properties under different grazing intensities remain elusive. This study examined variations in plant community characteristics, including biomass, quantitative traits, and species diversity, under a gradient of grazing intensities. Species were classified into functional groups, and their corresponding soil physicochemical properties were analyzed. The results showed that aboveground biomass was highest under no grazing and light grazing, and lowest under extreme grazing. Height and coverage of annual and biennial forbs and perennial grasses declined sharply with increasing grazing intensity. Species richness and diversity indices reached their minimum values under heavy grazing, while Simpson's dominance index peaked. Soil analysis revealed that available nitrogen and available phosphorus declined with increasing grazing intensity. Pearson correlation analysis revealed positive relationships between available nitrogen, available phosphorus, and plant α‐diversity, biomass, and basic traits. Structural equation modeling further showed that grazing not only directly affected plant communities but also influenced them indirectly through reductions in soil available nitrogen and available phosphorus. In conclusion, regulating grazing intensity to maintain soil nutrient availability may be important for sustaining the stability and functioning of desert steppe ecosystems.
n9f491417f525: Environmental conditions vary longitudinally along a river continuum, shaping the structure and functioning of biological communities, as explained by the River Continuum Concept. Riparian zones are important transitional areas linking the aquatic and terrestrial ecosystems. Therefore, a meta‐ecosystem perspective predicts that the longitudinal patterns described by the RCC extend into riparian habitats, leading to systematic change in terrestrial communities. We conducted a field study on near‐natural forested sections of five streams in southwestern Germany, sampling spiders in the up‐, mid‐ and downstream sections. We examined how variation in aquatic and terrestrial abiotic parameters among stream sections influences riparian spider diversity and community composition using pitfall traps and hand‐catches. Spider abundance increased along the stream course, whereas alpha diversity remained unchanged, suggesting that larger and more extensive riparian habitats in midstream and downstream reaches support higher population densities through greater habitat quality and resource availability without increasing local species richness. Despite similar levels of alpha diversity, each stream section harbored a distinct spider community composed of varying proportions of riparian specialists and habitat generalists. Correspondingly, spider trait composition changed markedly along the stream course: upstream reaches were characterized by heterogeneous communities with a high proportion of shade‐tolerant and web‐building species, whereas midstream reaches were more homogeneous and dominated by large‐bodied active hunters. Downstream communities were again more heterogeneous and contained many web‐building and open land‐preferring species. In contrast, spider moisture preferences remained largely unchanged along the stream course. Our findings enhance the understanding of how environmental longitudinal gradients shape riparian habitats and communities under near‐natural conditions, a fundamental step in understanding human impacts on riparian biodiversity.
nb235b15bd927: Assessing habitat use, spatial distribution, and site fidelity is critical for the conservation of threatened marine species, yet monitoring rare and elusive species in these types of complex environments remains difficult. This limitation is particularly critical for dugong (Dugong dugon) populations in the Western Indian Ocean, which are extremely small, fragmented, and difficult to monitor, posing a major conservation challenge. This pilot study aimed to develop a cost‐effective and field‐optimized eDNA workflow based on species‐specific qPCR for large‐scale monitoring of this threatened sirenian in shallow tropical coastal ecosystems. Field sampling was conducted in Mozambique, which hosts the only remaining large dugong population in the region. Using a species‐specific qPCR assay independently developed and validated for this study, we evaluated how sampling design and sample processing influence dugong eDNA detection under natural conditions. n1d6c9e13a184: Although the Varroa destructor mite is the primary threat to honey bee (Apis mellifera), populations of A. m. simensis in Ethiopia naturally survive mite infestations without treatment. n77acba8a7347: Wild bee populations are declining due to habitat loss and degradation.
