n245863c62ec9: By evaluating the effects of burned habitats on the habitat selection and movement responses of cougars and mule deer, cougar kill sites, and mule deer reproduction, the authors find that increasingly large, severe burns are diminishing herbivore reproductive success, potentially due to advantages for predators created by burned landscapes. Abstract Intensifying wildfire regimes under global change are expected to shift species interactions through changes in habitat structure and composition, vegetation productivity, and sensory cues. Yet there is little evidence of how burn‐induced changes in habitat composition and structure modify predator–prey relationships. We investigated how wildfires influence relationships between mule deer (Odocoileus hemionus) and cougars (Puma concolor) in the US Intermountain West using high‐resolution telemetry data, kill site locations, and annual measures of mule deer fawn production. Burned habitats experienced a wide range of fire severities, and most fires occurred between 5 and 20 years prior to animal data collection. We found that cougars were located closer to deer and their kill sites were nearly 2× more likely to occur in burned areas compared to unburned sites, suggesting that burns confer advantages to predators. In addition, fawn production declined by up to 14% at sites with histories of more recent, higher severity burns. Our findings suggest that increasingly frequent, severe burns are diminishing herbivore reproductive success, potentially due to increasing predation risks that outweigh improved foraging opportunities for prey. Ultimately, we reveal a possible pathway through which changing fire regimes could threaten herbivore prey populations in Western US ecosystems.
n18b2408fe992: This study extends ecological theory on facilitation to marine soft-sediment systems and offers insight into the functional role of habitat-forming infauna. Abstract Positive species interactions, or facilitation, are fundamental drivers of ecological community assembly and stability. In terrestrial plant-dominated systems, the effects of facilitation on biodiversity have been shown to intensify along environmental stress gradients; however, comparable examples are absent for marine soft-sediment ecosystems (particularly those with animal facilitators), hindering progress in expanding ecological theory. Using a multi-site field experiment, we investigated the role of an intertidal infaunal clam (Austrovenus stutchburyi) as a community-level facilitator of macrofaunal species diversity across gradients of hydrodynamic forces acting on the seabed (wind waves and tidal currents). Strong density-dependent influences of the clam on seabed stability were expected to be central to facilitation. At 21 intertidal sites across 4 estuaries in Aotearoa New Zealand, we removed adult clams from 9 m2 plots (removal plots) and then, after 12 months, measured the difference in macrofaunal community composition, richness and abundance between removal and adjacent non-removal plots. After 12 months, differences in macrofauna biodiversity between removal and non-removal plots were observed, and at some sites, these differences were associated with non-removal plots supporting up to 9× higher macrofauna abundance and up to 4× higher species richness than removal plots, indicating facilitation by Austrovenus as important for community composition. Facilitation was strongest at sites with high adult Austrovenus density (linear model R 2 = 0.52) but also proximity to strong tidal currents (polynomial model R 2 = 0.52), indicating that Austrovenus may extend macrofaunal communities into locations where they would otherwise be excluded by hydrodynamic forces. Synthesis: Our results provide evidence that the strength of facilitation in intertidal soft-sediments changes across hydrodynamic stress gradients; however, there are likely to be interactions between indirect and direct effects that we discuss in the context of our study system. Our study extends ecological theory on facilitation to marine soft-sediment systems and offers insight into the functional role of habitat-forming infauna.
n2bf8a4d2dafd: The relationship between species abundance and plant–soil feedback depends on the local density of each species. Our shade‐house experiment detected a negative abundance–feedback relationship only under high local density, with soil fungal pathogens potentially contributing to this pattern. These findings highlight local density as an important spatial context for interpreting contrasting feedback patterns in forest communities. Abstract Increasing evidence suggests that plant–soil feedback (PSF) is essential in shaping species abundance and promoting the coexistence of common and rare species. Yet, empirical studies have yielded inconsistent results regarding the relationship between species abundance and PSF strength. To reconcile the debate on the species abundance–PSF relationship (SAPR), we propose a conceptual framework that decomposes PSF into two components: PSF1 caused by the focal tree and PSF2 caused by the conspecific neighbours. These two components drive community assembly and diversity maintenance processes, respectively. Moreover, our framework emphasizes that local conspecific density is critical for measuring species PSF in natural communities. We then conducted a shade‐house experiment involving 14 subtropical tree species to test the SAPR in a subtropical forest. We found a significant negative relationship between species abundance and PSF only when inoculum soils were collected from areas with high local conspecific density. The fungal pathogens in the soil and roots were identified as the key drivers of this pattern. Our study provides direct experimental evidence that local conspecific density affects the SAPR, which may clarify discrepancies across studies and advance our understanding of how PSF contributes to species coexistence in forest ecosystems. Synthesis. Integrating a conceptual framework with a multi‐species soil inoculation PSF experiment, we reveal intensifying negative PSF from rare to common species in a subtropical forest community, with local conspecific density influencing this pattern. Consequently, our study suggests that the intricate relationship between species abundance and PSF is closely implicated in the dynamics of local species coexistence. We propose that previous controversies regarding the SAPR primarily stemmed from the neglect of local species density and the confusion of distinct ecological processes across studies.

na61e5fbf0ece: There is growing recognition that shifting environmental conditions can alter the nature and potential benefits of plant‐microbe interactions. n65cc6680384e: Examples of floral trait divergences between sister species adapted to different pollination modes. More broadly, soil fungi act as ecological filters shaping bacterial assembly and may foster increasingly positive associations with bacteria in hyphal‐dominated habitats.
n64761aa22933: Overlapping niches and life habits of rootless vascular plants. Summary The evolution of roots was an instrumental event in the colonisation of land by vascular plants. Roots have undergone extensive radiation and can take many diverse forms including taproots, fibrous roots, and adventitious roots. This includes specialist root types, such as pneumatophores in mangroves, that have allowed species to occupy new ecological niches. In some cases, the relationship between roots and soil has been broken, rendering roots unnecessary and ultimately resulting in loss of this organ in some species. We identify several ecological niches/life habits in which rootless vascular plants have evolved: aquatic environments, canopies, arid environments, and carnivory. Many of these plants are challenging to cultivate in a laboratory environment. The exception to this is duckweeds, which we propose as a powerful experimental model for studying organ loss in plants.
nf4e30c119877: Chilling stress destabilizes the PSI‐NDH supercomplex in cucumber thylakoid membranes. At normal temperature, the intact PSI‐NDH supercomplex supports NDH‐dependent ferredoxin (Fd) oxidation and electron transfer to the plastoquinone pool, thereby helping to prevent excessive reduction of the PSI acceptor side. During chilling stress, damage to LHCA associated with the supercomplex promotes PSI‐NDH destabilization and reduces NDH activity. The resulting impairment of Fd oxidation decreases electron sink capacity, enhances PSI over‐reduction, promotes reactive oxygen species (ROS) formation, and ultimately leads to PSI photoinhibition. Summary Chilling stress induces photosystem I (PSI) photoinhibition in cucumber (Cucumis sativus L.). This process is associated with insufficient activity of the chloroplast NADH dehydrogenase‐like complex (NDH). However, whether the importance of NDH can be generalized to other species and how NDH function is impaired remain unclear. We first examined whether NDH is essential for PSI protection under chilling stress using an NDH‐deficient rice (Oryza sativa L.) mutant. The NDH‐deficient rice exhibited pronounced PSI photoinhibition under chilling stress. By contrast, rice expressing flavodiiron protein (FLV), which functions as an alternative electron acceptor downstream of PSI, did not exhibit PSI photoinhibition under chilling stress, demonstrating that the electron sink capacity of NDH is important for PSI protection under chilling stress. Furthermore, in cucumber, chilling stress destabilizes the PSI‐NDH supercomplex, leading to NDH monomerization and a consequent loss of NDH activity. This NDH monomerization is likely attributable to chilling‐induced damage to the light‐harvesting complex Lhca, which mediates the association between PSI and NDH. Together, these results indicate that NDH protects PSI from photoinhibition under chilling stress, and that chilling‐induced destabilization of the PSI‐NDH supercomplex represents a key molecular mechanism underlying PSI over‐reduction and photoinhibition in cucumber.
nba43c2543c33: Species richness is markedly uneven across the tree of life, and traits have long been invoked to explain this pattern. Expanding phylogenetic and trait datasets enable broader comparisons, but trait–diversity associations alone do not reveal how differences in richness arose. We argue that such associations should be reframed as process hypotheses about three non-exclusive processes: lineage origin, access to ecological or geographic opportunity, and persistence. Mixed trait–diversity associations are expected when the same trait influences multiple processes whose relative contributions vary across contexts. This process-based framework makes alternative diversification histories explicit and specifies contrasting temporal predictions that can be evaluated with complementary evidence. It clarifies what findings would weaken each hypothesis and when available data leave alternative histories unresolved.
na95b88637584: Flowering times have long been a harbinger of the changing seasons and, more recently, of a changing climate. Among the cues that trigger flowering, precipitation timing has been relatively little-studied. Tsafon et al. show that the timing of precipitation shapes flowering in complex ways. Much work remains to disentangle this complexity.
na737b3a22750: Understanding the genetic underpinnings of cooperative and noncooperative breeding behaviors is critical for species of conservation concern. We investigated the genetic relatedness of Hawaiian Stilts (Aeʻo; Himantopus mexicanus knudseni), a threatened subspecies restricted to the Hawaiian Islands, in relation to nesting behavior, given recent behavioral observations of cooperative breeding, potential conspecific brood parasitism, and potential pairing of closely related individuals for nesting. Using RAD sequencing of blood and feather samples, we generated ~6800 SNPs for parentage and relatedness analysis. Observational data documented behaviors including cooperative incubation, helpers-at-the-nest, and potential conspecific brood parasitism, which are rarely reported in Charadriiformes. Parentage, genomic relatedness, and Bayesian phylogenetic analyses revealed instances of conspecific brood parasitism and potential extra-pair paternity. We also find evidence of inbreeding, with an overall F IS of 0.23 and close genetic similarity between some mates. Ecological constraints and limited dispersal opportunities may promote cooperative breeding, conspecific brood parasitism, and inbreeding in Hawaiian Stilts. These results underscore the importance of maintaining and restoring nesting habitat to reduce pressures that may otherwise intensify inbreeding in this recovering population but also highlight the behavioral flexibility and adaptive capacity in this species.
n30ee8e81ce1f: Read the free Plain Language Summary for this article on the Journal blog. Abstract Generalist species may be comprised of individual specialists. Individual specialization can impact disease transmission at shared resources by shaping contact patterns. Mathematical models of pollinator diseases that spread via flowers have shown that R 0 can be greatly amplified when each forager specializes on one flower species at a time with slow turnover. Yet, such behaviour has not been empirically demonstrated in generalist bumblebees. Here, we used palynology from sequential pollen loads of individual common eastern bumble bees (Bombus impatiens) to assess their foraging preferences over time. We used an automated monitoring system to greatly improve recapture rates, hence allowing a more complete characterization of each bee's foraging behaviours. Individuals in a bumblebee colony exhibited unique foraging repertoires of two to three flower species while the full-colony diet breadth was up to three times larger depending on time of year. Individual repertoires exhibited roughly 50% turnover, on average, over 10 days. Implications for disease transmission when individual repertoire sizes are greater than one may differ from specialization on a single flower species. Hence, we developed mathematical models where each bee has an effective repertoire size of two, and found that ignoring individual specialization still resulted in an underprediction of R 0, although to a smaller extent compared to a single-specialty model. Our results provide novel insights into the foraging behaviours of social bumblebees and improve predictions of how diseases are transmitted and persist in complex plant–pollinator networks. Read the free Plain Language Summary for this article on the Journal blog.
n3eb0d2f78cd1: By combining extensive body mass records with population‐wide migration counts spanning several decades, this study uncovers long‐term improvements in body condition associated with progressively milder winters, alongside earlier spring departure in an Arctic migrant, highlighting the importance of the full annual cycle in determining species' responses to climate change. Abstract Many migratory birds now reach their Arctic breeding grounds earlier in response to advancing springs and shifting nutrient peaks, either by departing earlier from non‐breeding grounds or by travelling faster. For dark‐bellied brent geese, there is limited potential to travel faster, as their spring migration is already among the fastest of Arctic geese and swans. Earlier departure would require reaching departure body mass earlier, either through a faster accumulation of energy stores during spring staging in the Wadden Sea or via adjustments earlier in the annual cycle. We examined long‐term shifts in spring staging phenology and changes in winter and spring body mass trajectories of brent geese at the population level, with particular emphasis on the effects of winter temperature on body mass and spring body mass on departure timing. We used more than five decades of body mass measurements from individuals caught in the United Kingdom and France and in the Dutch Wadden Sea to reconstruct changes in winter and spring mass trajectories, respectively. These data were combined with over five decades of migration counts in the Netherlands and more than two decades of counts in Denmark to quantify changes in arrival and departure timing, respectively. We found that brent geese were heavier during and after milder winters and that their body mass trajectories flattened over the years: they no longer lose body mass during winter; during spring staging, fuelling rates have declined (in the so‐called ‘fattening phase’), while they also no longer lose body mass in the 1–2 weeks prior to departure (‘plateau phase’). Brent geese have not shifted their spring arrival in the Wadden Sea but have advanced departure timing. Annual variation in body mass was not related to annual departure timing. These results suggest that milder winters have relaxed energetic constraints and improved body condition in brent geese throughout the non‐breeding season. Our findings highlight the importance of considering the full annual cycle when assessing how migratory animals respond to global change, in particular those with limited capacity to adjust migration timing or speed.
nb536505d1b66: These findings reveal that FGR provides a structural template for biotic resistance, whereas functional identity determines whether this template translates into resource pre‐emption or community vulnerability. In nutrient‐enriched ecosystems, low‐biomass legumes can inadvertently convert nutrient pulses into invasion opportunities by elevating the baseline resource environment and presenting limited above‐ground suppression. Restoring invasion‐resistant communities under N enrichment therefore requires functional‐identity screening—prioritizing strongly competitive non‐legumes rather than relying solely on FGR. Abstract Anthropogenic nitrogen (N) enrichment often promotes plant invasions by increasing resource availability, yet why resident communities differ in their resistance to the same resource pulse remains poorly understood. Here, we manipulated native plant functional group richness (FGR = 1–3) and community composition while holding species richness constant and assessed the performance of the nitrophilous invader Bidens alba under ambient and N‐enriched conditions to determine whether biotic resistance is driven by diversity per se or specific functional identities. N enrichment consistently increased invader biomass, but its interaction with FGR was not significant across the full richness gradient, indicating that FGR alone was insufficient for predicting biotic resistance. Instead, functional identity strongly governed plant invasion outcomes. Non‐legume communities (grasses and forbs) sustained high biotic resistance under N enrichment through strong above‐ground neighbour suppression. Conversely, legume‐containing communities exhibited weak biotic resistance under N enrichment, permitting a considerable increase in invader biomass. Legumes facilitated plant invasion through a coupled below‐ and above‐ground mechanism: they maintained a high baseline soil nitrate availability while experiencing competitive suppression under N enrichment, resulting in low biomass and minimal physical canopy presence. Combined with N enrichment, this created a favourable resource window that enabled B. alba to reduce its root: shoot ratio—a morphological plasticity response constrained in non‐legume communities by dense native neighbour biomass. Synthesis. Our findings reveal that FGR provides a structural template for biotic resistance, whereas functional identity determines whether this template translates into resource pre‐emption or community vulnerability. In nutrient‐enriched ecosystems, low‐biomass legumes can inadvertently convert nutrient pulses into invasion opportunities by elevating the baseline resource environment and presenting limited above‐ground suppression. Restoring invasion‐resistant communities under N enrichment therefore requires functional‐identity screening—prioritizing strongly competitive non‐legumes rather than relying solely on FGR.
n1b77f2412b3c: Ecogeographic generalizations or “rules”, such as Bergmann's rule and Allen's rule, propose that endotherms in colder climates evolve larger bodies and shorter appendages to minimize heat loss. These patterns are hypothesized to reflect physiological adaptations to thermal stress through reduced surface area‐to‐volume ratios. Although these rules have been extensively evaluated across birds and mammals, their applicability to arboreal gliders remains untested, with little consideration of how alternative ecological and evolutionary drivers may structure morphological variation in flying squirrels across environmental gradients. Using digitized museum specimens of North American flying squirrels (Glaucomys sabrinus, Glaucomys oregonensis, and Glaucomys volans), we tested these classic ecogeographic principles by examining how weight, total length, tail length, and ear length vary across a latitudinal gradient. We found significant support for Bergmann's rule, with body mass and total length increasing with latitude. In contrast, patterns in appendage morphology provided limited support for Allen's rule. Ear length exhibited a weak positive relationship with latitude, while tail length strongly increased with latitude, contradicting the prediction that appendages become shorter in colder climates. These findings suggest that thermoregulatory selection alone cannot explain morphological variation in North American flying squirrels and that functional demands, particularly those associated with gliding performance, may play a stronger role in shaping tail morphology. Overall, our results demonstrate that although classic ecogeographic rules provide a useful framework for understanding morphological variation, they do not fully capture the multiple selective pressures acting on Glaucomys species.
n94b38a81c4a0: Against the backdrop of ongoing urban expansion, alien plant invasions are closely linked to the stability of urban ecosystems. However, few studies have documented invasive plant distribution and their statistical associations with landscape variables in mountainous medium‐sized cities, which serve as critical urban–rural transition zones. This study selected Anning City, a representative mountainous medium‐sized city in Yunnan, Southwest China, as the research case. We established 63 standard sampling plots spanning urban, suburban, and exurban zones along an urbanization gradient. Canonical Correspondence Analysis (CCA) and Monte Carlo permutation tests were adopted to quantify statistical associations between six major macro‐environmental variables and invasive plant spatial distribution, and to characterize the distribution features of invasive plants for reference in targeted monitoring work. The main observations are summarized as follows: (1) A total of 66 alien invasive plant species belonging to 24 families and 51 genera were recorded. Asteraceae was the most abundant family, accounting for 25.75% of all taxa; 68.18% of species originated from the Americas, and annual and biennial herbs dominated the community (75.75%), which tend to occur abundantly in frequently disturbed habitats. (2) This local dataset captured a site‐specific trend where invasion abundance declines as urbanization intensity rises: the total number of invasive species increased from urban to suburban and exurban zones, yet significant gradient differentiation only existed in plant abundance rather than species richness. Suburban and exurban plots had similar abundance values (p > 0.05), and both presented significantly higher invasive abundance than urban plots (p < 0.001). Dense invasive aggregations were frequently detected along transportation corridors and rural land, while forested areas generally corresponded to lower invasive plant coverage. (3) Invasive plant distribution displayed combined statistical associations with multiple environmental variables. Building density presented the strongest correlation with community composition (p = 0.004), while urbanization gradient, terrain attributes, and population density also showed significant associations; no meaningful statistical links were detected for road network density and land‐use type. Widespread and common species exhibited significant correlations with macro‐environmental predictors, whereas rare species showed no such associations. Collectively, this paper describes the site‐specific distribution features of invasive plants and their correlated landscape variables in mountainous medium‐sized cities of Southwest China. This work supplements case evidence for invasion ecology research in moderately urbanized mountainous regions and offers empirical references for invasive plant surveillance in comparable subtropical mountainous medium‐sized cities globally.
nef34442bc0ae: The cockroach endosymbiont Blattabacterium cuenotii plays a central role in host nutrition throughout development, particularly during embryogenesis in the viviparous cockroach Diploptera punctata. However, the presence and potential functional relevance of non‐blattabacterial taxa in developing embryos of this species remain unclear. Previous studies of maternal and embryonic microbiomes in D. punctata, based on Illumina 16S rRNA sequencing, have yielded inconsistent findings, partly due to differences in how endosymbiotic sequences were treated. Here, we reanalyzed microbiome data from two studies, with and without Blattabacterial reads, to reevaluate the presence and composition of non‐blattabacterial taxa in embryonic microbiomes. Embryonic microbial communities (1) differed significantly from each other between datasets and (2) from associated maternal gut communities, suggesting that environmental (maternal, dietary, and laboratory) and sequencing factors may influence their acquisition and composition rather than reflecting a stable, consistently transmitted microbiome. Nevertheless, the detection of non‐blattabacterial taxa in embryonic microbiomes suggests the possible acquisition of non‐endosymbiotic bacteria by developing embryos. The functions of these microbes are speculated, but were not explicitly tested in this study and remain to be verified. Overall, our findings suggest that although non‐endosymbiotic embryonic bacteria may be environmentally acquired and variable, their biological relevance remains unresolved and cannot be determined from 16S amplicon data alone. This highlights the importance of investigating acquired non‐endosymbiotic bacteria and their potential functional roles in the development of viviparous cockroaches.
n8bb3394cea6d: Taxonomic bias, that is, the disproportionate attention given to some taxa relative to their diversity, continues to hinder innovation and the pursuit of generality in ecology and evolution. Yet, the factors shaping ecologists' and evolutionary biologists' choices of study organisms mostly remain a mystery. We propose a framework explaining researchers' taxonomic choices along three major axes, supported by evidence from a preregistered survey of 868 researchers' experiences. First, rational considerations, such as logistical ease and societal relevance, were associated with the choice of research organisms within major animal groups but rarely across them. Second, contextual factors, like the prominence of certain organisms within peer networks or early‐career exposure to specific taxa, were also associated with researchers' decisions about which organisms to study. Third, emotional factors, including taxonomic affinities, closely mirrored taxonomic patterns in the literature, indicating that they are a major driver of organism choice at broad taxonomic scales. Based on these findings, we suggest actions to mitigate taxonomic bias, including promoting (i) outreach initiatives featuring neglected taxa, (ii) taxonomically equitable education and (iii) taxonomically diverse research experiences.
n83687383f2dd: Tristan da Cunha (TDC) is a remote archipelago of four South Atlantic islands whose nearshore fish assemblages remain comparatively poorly studied. Genetic studies of such disjunct groups can provide valuable information on evolutionary history, taxonomy, and stock structure relevant for conservation and sustainable fishery management. Here, we address such topics in the Five‐finger (Nemadactylus monodactylus), an abundant nearshore fish harvested for subsistence at TDC, using a combination of mitochondrial control region sequencing and microsatellite analysis. Mitochondrial data, including publicly available data for Southern Hemisphere congeners, recovered four well‐supported clades. Three clades were polyphyletic, containing sequences previously assigned to N. macropterus or N. bergi, whereas one was newly described and may be endemic to TDC. These patterns add to evidence for a complex evolutionary history within Nemadactylus and suggest that current taxonomic designations warrant re‐evaluation. mtDNA also confirms colonisation of TDC by multiple lineages. Neither mtDNA nor microsatellites provided consistent evidence of genetic differentiation among islands, including between the distinctive Gough morphotype and the northern islands. These results are consistent with substantial archipelago‐wide connectivity, but the limited nuclear marker set means that weak structure cannot be excluded. We therefore regard a single archipelago‐wide population as a provisional working hypothesis rather than a confirmed management unit. Broader geographic sampling and genome‐wide nuclear data are needed to test species limits, reconstruct evolutionary history, and resolve fine‐scale population structure relevant to management.
ne2d665d5bccc: Blumea (Asteraceae) comprises about 100 species distributed across tropical Asia, Africa, and Australia, many of which have medicinal value. However, morphological variation caused by hybridization has left the taxonomy of this genus unresolved. In this study, we assembled the chloroplast genomes of six Blumea species (B. repanda, B. axillaris, B. sinuata, B. martiniana, B. megacephala, and B. formosana) and compared them with those of four published species (B. oxyodonta, B. tenella, B. aromatica, and B. balsamifera). The six new plastomes are similar in size (150,783–151,281 bp), with a typical quadripartite structure, each containing 131 genes (86 protein‐coding genes, 37 tRNAs, and 8 rRNAs). Comparative analyses revealed conserved genome architecture, stable IR/SC boundaries, and no rearrangements. Six non‐coding and four coding regions were identified as candidate DNA barcodes. A total of 395 dispersed repeats, 79 tandem repeats, and 547 SSRs were identified. Among the 59 preferred codons, 29 were high‐frequency (RSCU > 1), and 28 of these ended in A/U. Additionally, positive selection was detected in 21 genes, for example, ycf1, ycf2, rpoB, and ndhA. Phylogenetic analyses (ML and BI) based on 23 taxa (21 Inuleae species plus two outgroups) showed that Blumea is a highly supported monophyletic group (BS = 100%, PP = 1.00), internally divided into three subclades: subclade I (B. axillaris, B. oxyodonta, B. megacephala, B. repanda, B. sinuata, and B. tenella), subclade II (B. balsamifera), and subclade III (B. aromatica, B. formosana, and B. martiniana), with the latter three species all belonging to Section Macrophylla. These genomic resources lay a foundation for future phylogenetic, population‐genetic, and biotechnological studies of Blumea.
nde531f221655: Floral colour change can signal floral state, but its role in rainforest canopy trees remains poorly understood. We investigated colour change and pollinator visitation in Firmiana daweishanensis, a Plant Species with Extremely Small Populations endemic to southeastern Yunnan, China. Using a 25‐m scaffold, we observed 16 flowering branches on one adult tree for 128 branch‐hours. We combined these observations with measurements of linalool emission, nectar accumulation, reproductive function, calyx reflectance and bee visual modelling. Six hymenopteran taxa visited the tree, with Megachile bees dominating visitation. Mixed models showed that yellow flowers received more visits and greater cumulative visitation time per flower‐hour than red flowers within both sexes. Neither the omnibus sex tests nor the colour × sex interactions were significant. Branch‐level floral abundance and colour composition were not significantly associated with visitation. This contrast was consistent with, but did not demonstrate, selection at a fine spatial scale; limited statistical power remained an alternative explanation. Yellow flowers showed higher linalool emission and stronger modelled green‐receptor contrast against a green background. Nectar availability and reproductive function were generally greater during earlier floral stages. Neither pollinator‐excluded nor artificially geitonogamously self‐pollinated flowers produced fruit, whereas naturally exposed flowers showed 6.19% fruit set. These observations support a contribution of floral visitors to fruit set, but the absence of a hand‐cross‐pollinated control prevented a conclusive assessment of self‐incompatibility. Because colour, age, scent, reward and reproductive state covaried, their individual contributions to visitation could not be distinguished. Floral colour change may therefore form part of a multimodal indicator of floral state, while any display function of retained red flowers remains hypothetical. This within‐tree case study documents canopy visitation patterns whose generality requires replication across individuals and populations.
nc5f89cf613ea: The olive tree is one of the most important crops in the world, but even more, one of the most identitarian plant for the countries of the Mediterranean basin. In this article, the vast consultation of scientific literature, archaeological, historical and anecdotal sources, allowed to outline a global reasoned vision on the olive origin, its spread during early history and how olive fruit fly may represent as proxy for tracing its early diffusion. The reconstruction of the first forms of exploitation, propagation and trade routes yielded a chronologically coherent westward emergence of integrated olive-oil economies and cultures throughout the Mediterranean Basin, with the exception of some independent cultivation events tied to the widespread diffusion of the wild olive tree from the end of the last Glacial Period. Written sources, iconography, and archaeological installations further anchor this spatio-temporal narrative, leading to the transition from -wild- olives gatherers to olive growers.
nadf937bb6246: Read the free Plain Language Summary for this article on the Journal blog. Abstract The ability to detect prey is crucial for survival in many animals. However, prey detection is a cognitive process that can be influenced by early life conditions such as prenatal stress or temperature. Mitochondrial function is likely to underlie these effects because cognitive abilities are energetically demanding (i.e. dependent on efficient metabolic function) and because metabolic‐derived oxidative stress and oxidative damage can impair cognitive function. Yet, whether prenatal stress and thermal environments affect prey detection, and whether mitochondrial function mediates such effects, remains poorly understood. Here, we investigated the links between prenatal environments, mitochondrial function and prey detection in the delicate skink (Lampropholis delicata). We manipulated egg corticosterone (CORT) levels—a key stress hormone in reptiles—and incubation temperature and assessed the ability of lizards to detect chemical and visual prey stimuli. Then, using flow cytometry, we measured metabolic function, oxidative stress and oxidative damage in the olfactory bulbs and optic tecta, two brain regions involved in sensory processing. While metabolic function and oxidative stress remained robust to early life conditions, CORT and temperature interacted to influence oxidative damage. Particularly, CORT decreased DNA damage in the olfactory bulbs of cold‐incubated lizards but had no effect on hot‐incubated lizards. In both brain regions, lipid peroxidation was lower in CORT‐treated lizards incubated at high temperatures compared to CORT‐treated cold‐incubated lizards, but no other between‐treatment differences were detected. Additionally, CORT‐treated lizards responded faster when presented with chemical cues but not visual stimuli. We did not find any relationship between mitochondrial function and prey detection. Our findings suggest that prenatal conditions have lasting effects on DNA damage and prey detection, but prey detection appears decoupled from mitochondrial function in L. delicata. Read the free Plain Language Summary for this article on the Journal blog.
nf16574882ff3: The timing of biological events for wildlife species reflects and influences ecological and evolutionary processes and helps guide management actions to meet conservation objectives. Climate change may cause phenological shifts across trophic levels and ecosystems, which can have broad ecological impacts. Shifts may also result in mistiming between management practices based on historical conditions and current biological events, reducing the effectiveness of natural resource management and conservation efforts. We analyzed nesting phenology patterns over recent decades across North America for 44 species of grassland‐nesting birds, including waterfowl, upland gamebirds, shorebirds, and passerines, many of which have experienced precipitous population declines. Understanding nesting phenologies of these species is important to their conservation, as grassland management activities often conflict with reproductive periods leading to high nest and young mortality. We compiled a dataset of over 172,000 nest records spanning five decades and evaluated environmental factors influencing long‐term shifts and short‐term flexibility in nesting phenology. We found considerable variation in responses among species, with differences in both direction and magnitude of spatiotemporal effects on nest initiation dates. Notably, the community‐level nesting season lengthened over time, but shifts exhibited spatial heterogeneity within this community of grassland birds. Nesting dates shifted asymmetrically across the breeding season with differential changes in early, peak, and late nesting dates whereas long‐term changes were mediated by weather and geographic gradients. For example, nest initiation was earlier in warmer and wetter years. By applying a quantile‐based analysis, we provide estimates of the full nesting period that could serve as a flexible tool for scheduling monitoring efforts and balancing management and human activities with periods of reduced nesting activity. Our collaborative effort illustrates the challenges and opportunities of collecting long‐term data on avian communities necessary for answering questions across large regions but highlights the value of research coordination for bird conservation.
nfdc10a66d1a6: Using individual‐level nemabiome metabarcoding of 3147 samples from 916 horses on Sable Island over 10 years, we generate the largest dataset of its kind to date. This unprecedented scale enables a rare test of the processes structuring parasite communities in a natural system, revealing dominant host‐mediated filtering and predominantly positive species associations. Abstract Mixed‐species parasite infections are common in wildlife, yet the ecological processes that structure these communities remain poorly understood. We hypothesized that host‐mediated and extrinsic environmental filtering, alongside biotic interactions, act concurrently to shape parasite community composition, and that these structuring patterns would depend on parasite traits or evolutionary history. We applied nemabiome DNA metabarcoding to 3147 faecal samples from 916 feral horses with no history of anthelmintic treatment, collected over 10 years as part of a long‐term individual‐based study on Sable Island, Canada. Using joint species distribution models, we tested whether strongyle parasite communities were structured by host‐associated factors, extrinsic environmental variables or interspecific interactions. Host factors, particularly age and individual identity, explained the greatest proportion of variation in both parasite prevalence and infection intensity, indicating strong host‐mediated environmental filtering. In contrast, spatial location and year explained minimal variation, suggesting weaker effects of extrinsically mediated environmental filtering. Parasite traits such as body size and gut site preference had limited associations with species' environmental responses. Positive species associations were common, particularly among species occupying the same gut region, suggesting that strong, consistent competitive interactions were not prominently reflected in the residual covariance structure. Negative associations were less frequent but consistently involved Strongylus equinus, indicating potential context‐dependent biotic interactions involving this species. By integrating species‐level molecular data with hierarchical joint species models, this study quantifies patterns of host‐related filtering and species co‐variation within a natural parasite community and provides a framework for examining mixed infections in wild systems.
n6f54bdec2b91: Observations of three‐dimensional (3D) coarse root system architecture remain limited because most measurement approaches require excavation. Here, we combined dense single‐ and multi‐channel 500 MHz ground‐penetrating radar (GPR) surveys with a flow‐guided connectivity framework to non‐destructively characterise the coarse root architecture of two trees. Migrated and depth‐normalised GPR amplitudes were treated as spatially variable hydraulic conductivities in a steady‐state numerical model. The resulting connectivity fields transformed spatially discontinuous, collapsed diffraction hyperbolae into continuous 3D representations of root architecture extending 10–15 m from the trunk. We applied this approach to a swamp oak (Quercus palustris) and a river red gum (Eucalyptus camaldulensis). The two trees were surveyed under different environmental conditions and acquisition parameters. The reconstructed architectures revealed shallow, laterally extensive coarse root systems and captured substantial variation in root structure between the two trees. The oak roots exhibited an asymmetrical architecture with preferential development towards the upslope, wind‐exposed side of the tree, whereas the river red gum displayed a more radially distributed root architecture with deeper roots near the trunk. Approximately 80% of reconstructed roots for both trees occurred within 6.2 m of the trunk and above 60 cm depth. Together, these results demonstrate that dense GPR surveys, coupled with connectivity‐based modelling, provide a non‐destructive and repeatable approach for characterising coarse root architecture.
n971acb888766: Modern marine surveys generate tens of thousands of underwater images per expedition, yet many are unusable due to image quality deterioration. Manual quality screening is labour-intensive, subjective and inconsistent across observers and teams, hindering reproducible science, creating large backlogs of unprocessed imagery, and limiting real-time algorithmic and robotic applications. We present UNIQAT (UNderwater Image Quality Assessment Toolkit), an open-source Python toolkit for automated underwater image quality assessment. The toolkit computes reference-free quality metrics across nine categories of image characteristics relevant to underwater images, such as colour cast, turbidity and contrast loss. Metrics can be combined with user-defined weights into task-specific quality scores tailored to different ecological applications. High-performance computing (HPC)-aware multiprocessing and optional deep learning architectures for metric approximation support processing at scales matching modern survey data collection. We evaluated UNIQAT on 130,845 images from nine coral reef surveys conducted by the Australian Institute of Marine Science; every result reported in the main text was produced by the traditional metrics pipeline, with no deep learning model involved, and a separate training demonstration is reported in the Supporting Information. The traditional metrics pipeline, run as 48 CPU workers on a 64-core cluster node, processed 7.9 4K-images/s, with processing time scaling linearly with image count (r 2 = 0.98). The resulting quality scores captured expected patterns of image modulation based on the environmental context of the imaged scenes: All nine surveys showed negative depth–quality correlations (r = −0.16 to −0.89), consistent with the depth-dependent deterioration of image quality in underwater environments. Cross-survey metric profiles were highly consistent (mean Spearman ρ = 0.99 across all 36 pairwise comparisons, minimum 0.96), confirming measurement stability across different dates, locations, camera systems and environmental conditions. Synthesis. UNIQAT can help deliver objective and tunable image quality metrics in a versatile toolkit that enables transparent reporting and supports unsupervised quality assessment for applications in marine monitoring and robotics.
n3a236738bca4: Conservation of biodiversity is a global priority as human‐driven pressures continue to intensify and alter ecosystems worldwide. Marine mammals are vulnerable species, facing numerous escalating anthropogenic threats. Here, we evaluate how, as omics technologies become more accessible and affordable, established and emerging tools are advancing effective marine mammal research and conservation management. Assessments of genetic diversity, adaptive capacity, demographic history and local adaptation provide vital insights into how marine mammal populations respond to environmental change across contemporary and evolutionary timescales. Whole‐genome sequencing, functional genomics, epigenetics and multi‐omic integration enable deeper insights into the molecular basis of complex fitness‐related traits. Approaches like epigenetics, ancient DNA and environmental DNA offer new opportunities to study cryptic, rare, or historical populations and evolutionary processes. Yet, effective marine mammal conservation management cannot rely exclusively on increased availability of omics tools and data. We emphasize the need and obligation for genuine collaboration and integration of Indigenous perspectives with marine mammal genomics approaches to foster ethical, inclusive and effective conservation, and suggest best practices for this. Additionally, we highlight that translating omics data into practical conservation outcomes remains challenging, requiring clear communication, collaboration and integration into management. Using marine mammal genomics to address conservation challenges in a changing world requires innovation, partnership and the integration of diverse knowledge systems, such as Indigenous Ecological Knowledge.
n6f520f3491cf: Global temperature anomalies increasingly disrupt the cnidarian‐algal symbiosis resulting in a phenomenon termed bleaching. In contrast to heat stress, the mechanisms underlying symbiotic breakdown under cold stress remain largely unknown. Combining physiological and metabolomic measurements, we investigated the response of the photosymbiotic sea anemone holobiont Aiptasia couchii to an experiment mimicking a cold spell in the Mediterranean Sea. Within 4 weeks, we observed the onset of symbiotic breakdown reflected in reduced algal endosymbiont density and chlorophyll a content. While photosynthetic efficiency remained largely unaffected, no gross photosynthesis was detectable in cold‐stressed anemones and decreases in glycosyldiacylglycerols and fatty acyl glycosides indicated chloroplast lipid remobilization. Hence, while cold and heat stress may invoke contrasting physiological effects on endosymbionts, our results suggest that both stressors destabilize the symbiosis through similar mechanisms culminating in host starvation.
n6cb410d3fe46: The mechanisms driving the megadiversity of parasitic wasps remain a central question in evolutionary ecology. na9df61126ecd: Biodiversity research has long focused on the number and identity of species, but recent advances suggest that ecosystem functioning depends on how species are connected. Predicting the consequences of biodiversity loss in the Anthropocene will therefore require moving beyond inventories of species toward a predictive ecology of interaction networks.

Abstract The intensity, frequency and severity of drought events are projected to increase in the Mediterranean region under ongoing climate change. This may impact plant growth and survival in Mediterranean forests leading to altered ecosystem dynamics. The functional diversity of soil macrofauna may have a critical role in mitigating negative climate change effects as it determines soil structure and regulates biogeochemical cycling as well as water retention. However, very little is known on how changes in climate and soil biodiversity conjointly influence plant growth. Individual macrofauna groups had stronger effects than overall functional diversity. Endogeic earthworm presence was associated with greater ecosystem‐level fine root and total plant biomass, but with lower fine root and total biomass in A. unedo. Diplopod presence was associated with greater stem diameter and higher total tree biomass in Q. pubescens. Overall, four consecutive summers of intensified drought had few significant effects on tree growth and biomass production, possibly because of high variability among individual trees. These results show that macrofauna effects on tree growth depend on both macrofauna group and tree species identity. Read the free Plain Language Summary for this article on the Journal blog.
n02cbb93f7dc6: Horizontal gene transfer (HGT) has profoundly shaped eukaryotic organellar genomes like plant mitochondria. na1ed1e5d3a12: Inbreeding depression can have major negative effects on both individual fitness and population performance. The only adult fitness trait affected, male extra‐pair paternity, is highly variable and under strong sexual selection. Our findings suggest that natural populations experiencing high effective population sizes and regular dispersal might be less affected by inbreeding depression than previously assumed based on studies of often insular and smaller populations.

Abstract Multi‐strata forests can enhance ecosystem functioning, with interactions between overstorey trees and understorey shrubs playing a pivotal role. However, how the structure and composition of neighbouring trees, together with shrub traits, influence shrub growth remains poorly understood. In a large‐scale subtropical biodiversity experiment manipulating tree and shrub species richness, we inventoried 4411 shrubs and their surrounding trees after 11 years of interactions. We found that individual shrub biomass declined with increasing neighbour tree species richness, basal area and functional diversity, but exhibited a U‐shaped trend with the proportion of ectomycorrhizal‐associated neighbour tree individuals. Shrubs with more conservative resource‐use strategies attained higher biomass, particularly when surrounded by trees with low functional diversity and a high proportion of ectomycorrhizal associations. Biomass was also greater when shrubs were more resource‐conservative and functionally distinct from the neighbouring trees. Our findings highlight how shrub functional traits, combined with tree diversity, competition and functional traits, shape tree–shrub interactions, with shrubs benefiting more from resource‐conservative and functionally distinct traits relative to their neighbouring trees. nf78c5657189e: Why don't all birds lay early? Our 16‐year study of Manx shearwater behaviour shows that selection on breeding timing fluctuates among years. We also find that lay dates are influenced by persistent individual differences, variation in non‐breeding duration, and pair synchrony, potentially constraining breeding phenological advancement under ongoing climate change. Abstract The relationship between earlier laying and higher breeding success is well‐established in avian species. However, a wide distribution of breeding timings is often maintained within a population, and the causes and consequences of this variation require further exploration, particularly as many avian species advance breeding phenology in response to climate change. However, lay date was not determined solely by individual behaviour. In this long‐lived species with stable pair bonds, the arrival date of the second‐returning bird constrained advancement in laying. This study suggests that variation in breeding timing is maintained through the combined effects of fluctuating selection, persistent individual differences, variation in non‐breeding duration and pair‐level processes. n5ef022bba785: Fire is a fundamental process that structures community assembly and biodiversity patterns; however, altered disturbance regimes associated with anthropogenic change present a major threat to fire‐adapted systems. Reintroducing fire to increase pyrodiversity (spatiotemporal diversity in fire) has been identified as an important step in restoring fire‐adapted western temperate forests. Here, we utilize phylogenetic and taxonomic metrics to assess how pyrodiversity influences plant community assembly dynamics and diversity patterns in the central Sierra Nevada, California, USA. Compared to fire exclusion, regional taxonomic and phylogenetic diversity generally increased after fire. Further, with increased pyrodiversity, community assembly mechanisms diversified and occurrences of diverse plant lineages and local phylogenetic endemism increased, illustrating how evolutionary history influences responses of plants to pyrodiversity. These results demonstrate the importance of restoring mixed‐severity fire to these systems and how phylogenetic tools can provide a valuable way to understand and monitor restoration impacts.

Abstract Despite its critical importance for biodiversity conservation, population persistence in multiple habitats under climate change has rarely been evaluated using long-term demographic data. Furthermore, the drivers of population growth and the contributions of different demographic rates to population growth rates are likely to vary across habitats. Here, we parameterized size-dependent integral projection models (IPMs) using 23 years of data on the clonal salt marsh plant Spartina alterniflora in two habitats at eight sites in coastal Georgia (USA) to investigate spatiotemporal variation in population dynamics and the driving mechanisms. Compared with environmental factors, population density was the strongest predictor of asymptotic population growth rates (λ) of S. alterniflora in nearly all creekbank and mid-marsh habitats, with population dynamics exhibiting pronounced negative density dependence. Creekbank populations compensated for a low contribution of clonal reproduction number to population growth by increasing recruit size, resulting in effective demographic compensation and similar population fitness between habitats at most sites. Together, negative density dependence and demographic compensation acted as key mechanisms promoting population persistence, allowing most S. alterniflora populations to maintain positive cumulative population growth rates (λ c) across habitats. This study highlights the value of demographic analyses in clarifying population trends of species exhibiting high spatiotemporal variability and provides robust evidence for population persistence of salt marsh plants under climate change, emphasizing the crucial role of intrinsic population regulatory mechanisms in maintaining population stability. n9b497d2fbda4: Open‐canopy forests and woodlands are a foundational component of historically fire‐adapted landscapes, yet their persistence under contemporary climate and fire regimes remains poorly understood. Here, we leverage historical aerial photogrammetry integrated with contemporary satellite imagery to assess landscape change, vegetation transitions, and ecological stability over a century (1930s–2020s) for a large regional landscape of the Interior Northwest. We found woodlands declined by more than 40% across the region and exhibited high rates of type conversion, with roughly half converting to closed‐canopy forests and a quarter transitioning to grass‐ and shrub‐dominated ecosystems. Forest area, in contrast, remained relatively stable over the same period as woodland‐to‐forest conversion compensated for forest losses. The widespread decline in woodlands demonstrates that they exist as a metastable state, created and maintained only under stable, low‐ and mixed‐severity fire regimes. The loss of these keystone ecosystems portends the erosion of landscape resilience—as remaining woodlands disappear, their ability to buffer for forest losses will decline as well, increasing the risk of abrupt and persistent ecosystem transitions under shifting fire regimes and warmer future climates.
n72db17948acc: The ‘genetic paradox of invasions’ refers to successful invasive populations originating from low founder numbers. Theory predicts that such invaders should exhibit reduced genetic diversity and increased inbreeding, which should restrict their evolutionary potential and often lead to inbreeding depression. Here, we provide evidence for an invader succeeding against these odds by demonstrating strikingly strong inbreeding in a highly successful, invasive freshwater mussel. Using whole‐genome resequencing data, we show that zebra mussels (Dreissena polymorpha) from thriving invasive populations carry numerous and long runs of homozygosity (ROH) in their genomes, reflecting severe, sequential founder events followed by inbreeding during the invasion process. These genomic consequences of inbreeding would be expected to decrease the fitness of invasives, but here have not prevented their success. Our study thus challenges conventional expectations that inbreeding and high numbers of putatively deleterious alleles should limit biological invasion success. This research provides a compelling example of an invader that defies genetic expectations, and is therefore broadly relevant for understanding invasion success and dynamics across taxa.
n117e08afe26e: The fungal pathogen Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis (Bd) has driven severe amphibian declines across the Neotropics, yet some species persist under enzootic pathogen conditions following epizootics. Putative Bd‐inhibitory bacteria were detected in all host species and occurred at greater relative abundance during the dry season and in species with aquatic larvae, but neither their richness nor abundance was associated with Bd infection or load. Mucosome assays showed little to no inhibition of Bd growth in most species; only Pristimantis laticlavius, one of the few species whose abundance increased following the historical Bd epizootic, exhibited slight inhibition. Integrating host immune traits, pathogen characteristics, and environmental conditions will be necessary to understand long‐term host–pathogen coexistence in this threatened amphibian community.
n13e77e5724a5: Understanding the mechanisms driving genetic differentiation—and ultimately, speciation—is central to evolutionary biology, particularly in widespread species inhabiting environmentally complex landscapes. Homonota darwinii, a member of the H. whitii group, is the southernmost gecko in the world, distributed across the Patagonian Steppe—a vast, heterogeneous landscape with a complex geoclimatic history. This system offers an opportunity to assess the relative roles of geographic distance, environmental variation, and landscape resistance in diversification. Genomic data revealed geographically consistent groups and admixture in transitional zones. We identified three putative species‐level lineages corresponding to regional phylogeographic breaks shared by other taxa. Landscape genomic analyses indicated that isolation‐by‐environment (IBE), particularly climatic gradients related to aridity, temperature, and seasonality, was the primary driver of genetic divergence. This study highlights the interplay of spatial, ecological and historical factors in shaping genetic structure and adaptation. It also provides a framework for taxonomic and conservation initiatives, especially given prior projections of climate‐driven population decline in H. darwinii.
nd0d111a0aac0: Habitat fragmentation is a leading cause of plant extinctions, yet predicting which species are most vulnerable remains a key challenge. We propose that population connectivity, and thus gene flow via pollination and seed dispersal, can be inferred from plant traits. We integrate these traits into a connectivity–trait dimension, which, together with breeding system, life-history traits, and landscape context, ranks species at risk of genetic erosion and local extinction, providing an early-warning triage tool. By linking traits to gene flow mechanisms, the framework helps prioritise investment in detailed population genetic analyses and provides a scalable tool to identify species most at risk of genetic inbreeding and extinction in fragmented landscapes.
nadd6ba2e1a80: IntroductionCoastal social-ecological systems face climate change, resource exploitation, and fragmented governance. Hazard-specific assessments cannot fully represent their capacity to cope with uncertain disturbances, while connections between nationally consistent screening and fine-scale local diagnosis remain limited.MethodsDrawing on general resilience theory, we developed a three-tier, ten-attribute framework linking a national baseline with a nested assessment in Rongcheng. Coastal land and marine subsystems were evaluated using a nominal 2025 temporal window that incorporated the closest reliable products for slowly updated variables. The analysis included indicator standardization, scale-specific weighting, composite assessment, Jenks natural breaks classification, and spatial autocorrelation analysis.ResultsThe mean general resilience capacity indices were 0.359 for national coastal land and 0.470 for national coastal waters. Low and relatively low classes accounted for 39.75% of national coastal land, whereas moderate and relatively high classes accounted for 65.48% of national coastal waters. In Rongcheng, moderate and relatively low classes jointly represented 68.30% of coastal land. Relatively low and relatively high classes accounted for 56.33% of coastal waters, with a coefficient of variation of 0.282, indicating pronounced intra-bay heterogeneity.DiscussionThe national assessment provides a consistent baseline for broad-scale screening, whereas the Rongcheng assessment identifies bay- and shoreline-scale units for future field verification. Because the assessments differ in indicators, weights, and spatial supports, their results should be interpreted within their respective scales rather than compared directly. Scale-matched monitoring and governance feedback can connect national screening with local diagnosis.
nfdbf090acb5f: Understanding the species composition and structural dynamics of both common and rare species in forest communities is fundamental to comprehending forest ecosystem functioning. The intake area of the South-to-North Water Diversion Project, recognized as an ecologically sensitive region, harbors forest communities that play a pivotal role in water resource conservation and regional environmental stability. Common species exhibited absolute dominance in both individual abundance and importance value. (2) Species accumulation curves showed a sharp increase in species number when plot counts were below 20, followed by a marked deceleration thereafter. (3) Common species dominated across all diameter and height classes, while rare species were largely confined to diameter class II (5 cm ≤ DBH < 10 cm) and height class III (6 m ≤ H < 9 m), indicating a conspicuous growth-stage bottleneck. (4) Common species were predominantly monoecious plant, whereas hermaphroditic species occurred mainly as rare species. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that common and rare species jointly underpin the stand structural integrity, species diversity, and long-term successional potential of the forest community in intake area.
nf2b714a8ec95: Read the free Plain Language Summary for this article on the Journal blog. Abstract Understanding whether land use intensification causes regime shifts (i.e. persistent, large changes in ecosystem states) is of key importance for management, particularly if these shifts occur abruptly as thresholds in land use intensity are crossed. Further, these threshold responses can show hysteretic dynamics, where the transition between states cannot simply be undone by reducing land use intensity to its initial level, and instead larger changes are required. However, quantitative evidence for threshold responses and their dynamics remain scarce. Here we use a unique, long‐term grassland database in Germany to identify threshold responses to land use intensity. We include data on the response of 16 ecosystem functions (including plant biomass, herbivory, litter decomposition, pathogen infection, water recharge, C and N fluxes and retention and enzymatic activity) and the diversity of 21 taxa (including above‐ground and below‐ground taxa such as vascular plants, lichens, bryophytes, arthropods, vertebrates, fungi, protists and bacteria). Then, we use increased variance as an early warning signal to evaluate if threshold responses are indicative of critical transitions between states. Finally, we use temporal data to identify hysteretic dynamics associated with those transitions. We show that 5 out of 10 above‐ground taxa, fungal diversity, shoot biomass and soil N retention showed threshold responses to land use intensity, that is abrupt changes between extensively and intensively managed grasslands. Some of the thresholds were associated with increased variance in the response variables, suggesting a potential critical transition between ecosystem states. Time‐series analysis indicated that ecosystem functions showed a hysteretic response to land use intensity, but diversity measures did not. Our results suggest threshold responses to land use intensity are relatively common in the grasslands we studied. These thresholds show abrupt changes in the ecosystem when highly diverse extensively managed grasslands are managed slightly more intensively. Further, shifting back to the functioning seen in extensively managed grasslands may be challenging, as it requires larger reductions in land use intensity than those required to shift to the high intensity state. Identifying thresholds along land use gradients is critical to prevent ecosystem degradation and conserve biodiversity and ecosystem functions in semi‐natural grasslands. n7657618aed79: Salt marshes are among the most valuable carbon sinks globally but are highly vulnerable to ongoing climate warming, which profoundly affects ecosystem photosynthesis and respiration and may therefore alter their CO2 sink capacity and efficiency. However, whether climate warming will enhance or reduce the function of salt marshes to act as CO2 sinks remains uncertain. Here, we investigated the interannual variations in salt marsh CO2 sink capacity (net ecosystem exchange, NEE) and efficiency (ecosystem carbon use efficiency, CUE) in response to climate warming, using a long‐term eddy covariance dataset (2011–2024) from the Yellow River Delta, supplemented by a manipulative warming experiment (2017–2021) and a multi‐site eddy covariance dataset spanning China and North America (68 site‐years). At the study site, we quantified multiyear mean values for NEE as −107 ± 59 g C m−2 year−1 and for CUE as 0.41 ± 0.16, both of which showed strong interannual variability. Moreover, rising temperatures were primarily and negatively associated with yearly changes in CO2 sink capacity and efficiency, and these relationships were closely linked to lower gross primary production. The warming experiment further showed that the warming‐induced reductions in CO2 sink capacity and efficiency were accompanied by increased soil salinity and reduced plant growth. Similar negative associations between temperature and both CO2 sink capacity and efficiency were also observed at several sites in the multi‐site dataset. Overall, this study improves our understanding of the coupling between climate warming and the CO2 sink function of salt marshes and suggests that continued warming may reduce net atmospheric CO2 uptake across this biome in the future.
nf3aa814d4ad2: Intercropping is a promising sustainable agriculture practice, but its adoption is hindered by the potential reduction in benefits when shifting from monoculture to intercropping, especially if there are trade‐offs between yield, soil organic carbon (SOC) and nitrous oxide (N2O) emissions. In this study, we synthesized 3843 paired observations from 510 field‐based studies that compared the yields, SOC and N2O emissions of intercropping systems (only crop‐crop intercropping for grain yield and including crop‐tree agroforestry in addition to crop‐crop intercropping for SOC and N2O) with monoculture systems. Legume‐based intercropping was found to be more effective than non‐legume intercropping. However, the effectiveness of intercropping systems varies depending on climate, soil properties and management practices. This conversion could also enhance SOC stocks by 2.84 Pg C yr.−1 and reduce N2O emissions by 625 Gg N yr.−1, resulting in a reduction of 10.6 Pg CO2‐eq yr.−1 for net global warming potential. Overall, converting monoculture systems to intercropping could generate approximately US$595 billion in economic benefits annually. These findings highlight the critical role of intercropping as a scalable nature‐based solution for addressing the dual challenges of global food security and climate change.
nd83ac8f1dd05: This study shows that projected ocean acidification does not alter behaviour or predation risk in coral reef fish, challenging earlier assumptions. By quantifying consistent individual‐level behavioural differences and relating individual traits to survival during a live‐predation trial, it also provides evidence for a boldness–predation trade‐off in a small‐bodied demersal fish. Abstract Ocean acidification, caused by rising carbon dioxide (CO2) in the atmosphere, has been reported to negatively impact a wide variety of behaviours in fishes, including activity, exploration, and predator avoidance. These effects have been documented at the population level, but many animal species naturally show large and repeatable individual‐level differences in behaviour. How environmental stressors, such as ocean acidification, affect behavioural variation at the individual level remains largely unknown but is vital in understanding adaptation given natural selection operates on variation at the individual rather than population level. Using a statistical approach allowing variation in means and variation in variance to be modelled within a single framework, we quantified individual‐level differences across five behaviours in the coral reef Ambon damselfish Pomacentrus amboinensis (emergence time, activity level, time spent sheltering, thigmotaxis and novel object inspection). We measured behaviour in a novel environment assay, twice before (CO2 ~450 μatm) and twice following 4–6 days of exposure to predicted end‐of‐century ocean acidification conditions (~1100 μatm). Following behavioural assays, we tested individual survival in a live predation experiment. We used predatory rock cod, Cephalopholis microprion, acclimated to the same CO2 treatments as Ambon damsels and examined predictors of survival probability. All behaviours in damselfish were moderately and significantly repeatable, with no marked differences in repeatability estimates between the ambient CO2 and elevated CO2 treatment groups. Exposure to end‐of‐century ocean acidification conditions had no effect on any of the five behaviours measured, both in terms of group means and residual (within‐individual) variance. The probability of survival in the predation trials was similar for damselfish in the ambient and elevated CO2 treatment groups. Smaller damselfish as well as those that spent a greater amount of time inspecting a novel object (i.e. bolder individuals) had a lower probability of survival regardless of their CO2 treatment. Our results challenge assumptions about the impacts of ocean acidification on coral reef fish behaviour and susceptibility to predation, both at the population and individual level. They also provide support for a trade‐off between boldness and predation risk in fish.
