Additionally, our findings can assist policymakers in identifying relevant but less common narratives in the biodiversity science–policy literature that may help them develop policies. El discurso científico de la pérdida de biodiversidad presentado con factores, soluciones y responsabilidades Resumen La pérdida de biodiversidad se considera un problema mundial de gran importancia, pero, al mismo tiempo, los científicos la interpretan de forma diferente, pues identifican diversos factores causales, soluciones y responsabilidades en sus trabajos publicados. Estas interpretaciones dan forma a las narrativas científicas que se utilizan para abordar la pérdida de biodiversidad, lo que a su vez influye en las políticas a través de la interfaz entre la ciencia y la política en materia de biodiversidad. Sin embargo, no existe una visión general completa de estas diferentes narrativas en la bibliografía sobre la pérdida de biodiversidad. Para llenar este vacío de conocimiento, realizamos una revisión bibliográfica de la literatura contemporánea y global sobre biodiversidad, así como un análisis de redes discursivas basado en los factores causales, las soluciones y las responsabilidades de la pérdida de biodiversidad. Identificamos siete narrativas que ofrecen una visión general del discurso científico sobre la pérdida de biodiversidad. Determinamos que las narrativas identifican diferentes factores clave de la pérdida de biodiversidad y, a menudo, se centran en los factores causales, las soluciones o las responsabilidades, mientras que algunas descuidan las dimensiones sociales. Además, nuestra investigación mostró que la categorización de los factores directos de la pérdida de biodiversidad, comúnmente utilizada por la Plataforma Intergubernamental Científico‐Normativa sobre Diversidad Biológica y Servicios de los Ecosistemas (IPBES), sólo se refleja en una de las siete narrativas, lo que indica su limitada prevalencia en la literatura. Por lo tanto, este estudio ayudará a los científicos especializados en biodiversidad a desarrollar narrativas más holísticas sobre la pérdida de biodiversidad, al reconocer las limitaciones de las narrativas que utilizan actualmente. Además, nuestros resultados pueden ayudar a los responsables políticos a identificar narrativas relevantes, aunque menos comunes, en la literatura científica y política sobre biodiversidad, que puedan servirles para elaborar políticas.
n9cb7b234e33e: Mammalian reproductive and glandular systems provide multiple routes through which maternal microorganisms can be transmitted to offspring, yet the evolutionary significance of these pathways remains incompletely understood. This manuscript proposes that mammalian evolution progressively incorporated microbial transmission into reproductive biology, increasing the fidelity with which beneficial host-associated microorganisms pass between generations. Under this framework, mammary glands evolved from ancestral apocrine-like glands to create sustained maternal–offspring interfaces through which microbial transmission could become an additional selectable function when host–microbe associations enhanced fitness. Comparative evidence from monotremes, marsupials, and eutherian mammals is examined through an apocrine–mammary–microbiota axis, encompassing glandular regulation of epithelial microbial communities, maternal microbial transmission during birth and lactation, and host mechanisms that selectively support microbial establishment. The term filial microorganism is introduced to distinguish microbial lineages whose intergenerational transmission is facilitated by evolved host mechanisms from microorganisms that are merely transmitted through maternal contact or environmental exposure. The framework is further extended, more speculatively, to the eutherian placenta, which is proposed to function not as a resident microbial reservoir but as a transient immunological interface capable of initiating low-abundance microbial founder populations during the physiological transition from pregnancy to birth. Subsequent exposure through the birth canal, maternal skin, glandular secretions, and lactation may then expand and refine these populations during early development. This hypothesis predicts that candidate filial lineages should exhibit preferential maternal transmission, persistence across host generations, evidence of host mechanisms facilitating their maintenance or transfer, and measurable contributions to host fitness. If supported, this framework would broaden mammalian inheritance beyond the transmission of host genes to include evolved biological mechanisms that preserve beneficial microbial partnerships across generations.
nd7a7aeda39a7: Roads affect wildlife through multiple pathways, including changes in abundance, activity, mortality, habitat use, and movement, yet these responses have rarely been synthesised within a common evidence framework. We fitted separate three-level meta-analytic models to 643 effects from 160 studies. On the log-response-ratio scale, road proximity was associated with approximately 32% lower wildlife outcomes (lnRR = −0.3872, 95% CI [−0.7293, −0.0452]). The standardized mean-difference estimate ( g = −0.1131, 95% CI [−0.2608, 0.0346]) and correlation-based estimate ( Z = 0.1691, 95% CI [−0.1915, 0.5297]) were both imprecise. Response-type patterns varied across metric families, indicating that road effects are expressed through distinct ecological pathways rather than as a uniform shift in all wildlife outcomes. Between-study heterogeneity was substantial, and prediction intervals included both reductions and increases across sites. Annual average daily traffic was available for 91 of the 643 analysed effects, representing 17 studies. Overall, roads were associated with heterogeneous wildlife responses, with the clearest average reduction observed on the ratio scale. More consistent reporting of traffic volume and road characteristics is needed to test transferable dose–response relationships.
n96723f693250: Read the free Plain Language Summary for this article on the Journal blog. Abstract Climate change and intensified fire regimes are reshaping ecosystems globally. Reptiles, as ectotherms, rely on microhabitat shelters to buffer against thermal extremes, yet the capacity of these shelters to persist or function following fire remains poorly understood. As heatwaves and fire regimes intensify under climate change, effective thermal buffering will become increasingly vital for reptile persistence. This study quantifies how fire alters the structure and thermal offset of key reptile refugia: spinifex (Triodia) tussocks, chenopod shrubs, and leaf‐litter mats, in the dune and swale habitats of South Australia's Murray Mallee. Using iButton data loggers deployed across four fire histories, we measured hourly microhabitat and adjacent ground temperatures, modelling thermal offset (Toffset) via mixed‐effects models. More recent fire histories were associated with less spinifex and leaf‐litter cover and more bare ground, although evidence for changes in individual shelter dimensions was mixed. Thermal buffering declined markedly in recently burnt sites, with long‐unburnt spinifex providing the greatest daytime protection from extreme ground temperatures. Structural properties such as tussock height and litter depth were associated with Toffset, supporting a relationship between shelter structure and thermal‐refuge quality. Comparisons with the thermal tolerance of spinifex‐obligate reptiles indicate that burnt habitats often exceed critical thermal limits, effectively eliminating usable refugia during heatwaves. These results demonstrate that fire‐driven structural simplification translates to weakened thermal refugia, with implications for species persistence under increasing heat extremes. Effective fire management in arid systems should, therefore, prioritise the protection and regeneration of long‐unburnt spinifex and litter habitats as critical microclimatic refuges. ndf20d30a0be2: This study demonstrates that specific ectomycorrhizal fungal taxa are associated with trade‐offs between greater tree growth and reduced soil carbon concentrations in boreal forests. This work presents field‐based evidence consistent with the emerging understanding that ectomycorrhizal fungi influence ecosystem carbon stocks through the enzymatic degradation of soil organic matter and uptake of organic nitrogen. Abstract Understanding the biological interactions which influence the boreal carbon (C) sink are critical to the development of accurate Earth System Models (ESM). Boreal forests are highly nitrogen (N) limited. To meet N demand, boreal trees associate with highly diverse ectomycorrhizal (ECM) fungal communities, which vary in their capacity to uptake recalcitrant organic forms of N. ECM acquisition of organic N has been suggested to positively influence tree growth, but the consequence of this activity on soil C pools is widely debated, with evidence for their activity both increasing and decreasing soil C. To evaluate the potential for ECM fungi to influence trade‐offs in above‐ and below‐ground C, we linked long‐term tree growth records (~25 years) of Picea glauca with individually paired molecular profiles of fungal communities inhabiting focal tree roots and surrounding soils. We conducted this study across a large climatic gradient in interior Alaska, along which we expected fungal community composition, N acquisitive properties and outcomes on C cycling processes to vary. We observed a ~90‐fold variation in tree growth. After accounting for co‐occurring climatic trends, we found that abundant ECM taxa linked with lower soil C concentrations were simultaneously associated with greater long‐term tree growth. We estimated outcomes of fungal community N acquisitive properties using foliar δ15N, finding that fungal community composition and particularly Cortinarius sequence abundance were significantly correlated with foliar δ15N. Synthesis. Ultimately, this work presents field‐based evidence consistent with the emerging understanding that ECM fungi influence ecosystem C stocks through enzymatic degradation of SOM and uptake of organic N. Specifically, our results support conceptualizations that ECM acquisition of organic N can contribute to trade‐offs in above‐ and below‐ground carbon storage by stimulating tree growth while reducing soil C accumulation. Efforts to promote a sustained boreal forest C sink require interrogating linkages between ECM community traits and their emergent effects on soil decay and tree growth.
nf6d2662d214c: Many ecological decisions are slowed by the gap between collecting and analysing biodiversity information. Edge computing moves data processing closer to the sensor, with edge artificial intelligence (AI) using AI models for data processing and selective data transfer. edge AI extends the scope of biodiversity monitoring by complementing retrospective ecological analysis with real‐time sensing, enabling responsive and adaptive decision‐making. However, the adoption of edge AI systems in ecological research remains fragmented because deploying efficient and reliable systems is complex. Edge hardware, on‐device AI models and network configuration are tightly linked, such that optimising any one component shapes the performance and feasibility of the others, demanding holistic system design. For the uptake of edge AI in biodiversity monitoring, it is essential to understand the design trade‐offs, performance constraints and implementation challenges faced by current systems. Here, we analyse 82 studies published between 2017 and 2025 that use edge AI systems for biodiversity monitoring across acoustic, vision‐based, tracking and multi‐modal sensing. We synthesise hardware platforms, AI model optimisation and wireless communication to assess how these design choices influence ecological inference and determine the practicality and longevity of field deployments. Annual publications rise moderately from 3 in 2017 to 19 in 2025. Across these studies, we identify four system types that represent distinct patterns of edge computing adoption in ecological monitoring. These include low‐power microcontrollers (MCUs) for single‐taxon or rare‐event detection (Type I: TinyML), single‐board computers (SBCs) supporting multi‐species classification and real‐time alerts (Type II: edge AI), distributed systems coordinating processing across multiple devices (Type III: Distributed edge AI) and network‐connected devices for cloud processing (Type IV: Cloud AI). Each type illustrates different trade‐offs among power consumption, computational capability and communication requirements. Our analysis reveals the evolution of edge AI systems from proof‐of‐concept to robust, scalable tools. We argue that edge AI systems enable timely and scalable ecological observations, but realising their full potential depends on closer collaboration between ecologists, engineers and data scientists to align AI model development and system design with ecological needs and field realities.
na1dca9e4f343: Geometric morphometrics (GM) is widely used to study phenotypic variation in ecological and evolutionary research, but the throughput of manual landmark digitization limits how large morphometric datasets can practically become, especially in field studies that would benefit from rapid on‐site feedback. We introduce Theia, an edge‐AI mobile framework that performs end‐to‐end GM workflows directly on‐device, including image acquisition, automated landmark detection and morphometric analysis. The system integrates a dual‐stage deep‐learning pipeline with an offline analytical engine implementing generalized procrustes analysis (GPA) and principal component analysis (PCA), enabling field‐based analyses on low‐cost mobile hardware. Validation against the geomorph R package demonstrated near‐perfect computational fidelity (|r| > 0.999). Comparisons with expert manual digitization across 268 held‐out specimens showed close morphospace concordance, with biological variation accounting for 92.9% of total shape variance and the method effect (AI vs. manual) for 0.5%. The method effect is small, so the shape ordination used in downstream analysis is preserved. Theia enables standardized, reproducible morphometric data collection directly in the field. It complements established desktop workflows and suits studies that need portability and on‐site quality control, such as large‐scale spatial sampling and long‐term monitoring. RESUMEN La morfometría geométrica (MG) se utiliza ampliamente para estudiar la variación fenotípica en investigaciones ecológicas y evolutivas. Sin embargo, el rendimiento limitado de la digitalización manual de puntos de referencia (landmarks) restringe en la práctica el tamaño que pueden alcanzar los conjuntos de datos morfométricos, especialmente en estudios de campo que se beneficiarían de disponer de información rápida in situ. Presentamos Theia, un sistema móvil basado en inteligencia artificial en el dispositivo (edge AI) que permite realizar flujos de trabajo completos de MG directamente en el propio dispositivo, incluyendo la adquisición de imágenes, la detección automatizada de landmarks y el análisis morfométrico. El sistema integra un proceso de aprendizaje profundo en dos etapas con un motor analítico que funciona sin conexión e implementa el Análisis Generalizado de Procrustes (GPA) y el Análisis de Componentes Principales (PCA), permitiendo realizar análisis directamente en el campo mediante dispositivos móviles de bajo coste. La validación frente al paquete geomorph de R mostró una fidelidad computacional prácticamente perfecta (|r| > 0.999). La comparación con la digitalización manual realizada por expertos en 268 especímenes independientes mostró una estrecha concordancia en el morfoespacio: la variación biológica explicó el 92.9% de la varianza totalde la forma, mientras que el efecto del método (IA frente a manual) explicó el 0.5%. El efecto del método espequeño, por lo que se conserva la ordenación de las formas utilizada en los análisis posteriores. Theia permite una recopilación estandarizada y reproducible de datos morfométricos directamente en el campo. Complementa los flujos de trabajo convencionales realizados en ordenadores y resulta especialmente adecuado para estudios que requieren portabilidad y control de calidad in situ, como los muestreos espaciales a gran escala y los programas de seguimiento a largo plazo.
nc93ad0526611: Soil protists comprise vast eukaryotic diversity and play key roles in microbial food webs, yet their community assembly remains poorly understood from a trait‐based perspective. Here, we address this gap by integrating 10 traits related to morphology, behaviour, life history and trophic strategy across broad environmental gradients. RLQ analysis combined with fourth‐corner tests revealed two major dimensions of soil protist trait variation. Reduced precipitation drove trait composition towards slower, persistence‐oriented strategies, including reduced mobility, narrower niche breadth and increased reliance on asexual reproduction. Nutrient and resource limitation shifted trophic structure away from heterotrophic consumer‐related strategies towards autotrophic or mixotrophic energy acquisition. These dimensions were consistently detected in a large‐scale field survey and broadly supported by an independent global‐change manipulation experiment, indicating that they capture generalizable components of soil protist functional organization. Further functional diversity analyses indicated that environmental gradients primarily constrained the range of occupied trait space rather than consistently reshaping the internal dispersion or evenness of trait distributions. Our study provides a trait‐based framework for predicting belowground community assembly and ecosystem functional responses to environmental change.
n42a25ecdf7b0: Body size is a master variable in ecology that can predict ecosystem‐level processes and reflect environmental conditions across diverse ecosystems. In freshwater ecosystems, the relationship between body size and biomass provides a powerful tool for characterizing community structure and trophic transfer efficiency. While these relationships are well established at the whole‐community level, responses within plankton functional groups with distinct ecological characteristics have yet to be explored. In this study, we analysed plankton biomass‐size relationships across > 550 Canadian lakes. For phytoplankton, we found that mixotrophs exhibited positive biomass‐size slopes, while autotrophs exhibited negative slopes. For zooplankton, herbivores exhibited relatively flat slopes, while non‐herbivores exhibited negative slopes. Biomass‐size relationships also differed among lake trophic states, but only for phytoplankton functional groups. This work should improve predictions and assessments of freshwater ecosystem functioning and food web pathways, based on our observation of directional shifts in biomass‐size relationships across functional groups and trophic states.
n509d4683da57: Soil salinization and sodicity are accelerating worldwide, reducing crop productivity across more than 160 million hectares of farmland and causing production losses approaching USD 27 billion annually. Despite decades of research documenting these impacts, the extent of salt‐affected soils continues to expand. Salt‐affected soil degradation emerges from feedbacks among physical, biological, and socioeconomic processes that operate across scales and resist intervention when addressed in isolation. This review synthesizes current understanding of these coupled feedbacks. We trace how ion accumulation, soil structural decline, microbial community disruption, and plant stress interact with irrigation practices, land use decisions, and governance systems. These interactions create threshold dynamics in which degradation can appear stable for years before rapid decline. Evidence from diverse regions reveals that effective restoration depends on coordinated interventions matched to the complexity of the system itself. Four research priorities emerge for advancing prediction and prevention. First, quantifying the thresholds that separate reversible from recalcitrant degradation across soil types and climates. Second, expanding predictive capacity through integrated sensor networks and data platforms that enable early warning. Third, improving understanding of how institutional structures influence adoption of restoration practices. Fourth, integrating biophysical and governance models to enable scaling from field trials to basin‐wide implementation. By coupling mechanistic understanding with monitoring infrastructure and adaptive governance, reactive remediation can give way to proactive prevention.
nbccc5cb2992c: Declining atmospheric sulfur (S) deposition makes S an emerging limiting macronutrient for plants, yet the stability and dynamics of soil organic S—the largest terrestrial S pool supplying plant‐available sulfate via mineralization—remain unclear. Across North American soils, total organic S is dominated by mineral‐associated organic S (MAOS; 61% ± 26%); this pool is stabilized by mineral protection but saturates at ~600 μg S/g soil. Compared with particulate organic S (POS), which is relatively labile and does not saturate, MAOS is more decomposed, chemically diverse, and climate‐sensitive. Higher temperature accelerates S mineralization in both pools, but their ability to supply available S varies with moisture regime because MAOS stabilizes in wetter soils while POS remains labile. This continental‐scale reassessment of the soil S cycle reveals that secondary minerals play a dual role in soil S cycling by stabilizing organic S and retaining sulfate, providing a mechanistic basis for nutrient management and carbon sequestration in response to climate change in an S‐scarce future.
n2966225831b8: Conspicuous colouration signals venomous nature throughout snakes. Abstract Many animals use conspicuous colours to advertise their unprofitability to potential predators, a phenomenon known as aposematism. For example, conspicuous banded patterns in snakes are often highlighted as aposematic signalling of their venomous nature. However, aposematic colouration needs to be analysed while considering a species' environmental context, seen as species which seem conspicuous in isolation may be well camouflaged within their natural environment. Here, we collate images for 458 snake species from iNaturalist and use a novel metric quantifying the degree of conspicuousness of each species compared with its natural context to test the relationship between conspicuousness and the presence, potency and defensive properties of venom. We find that venomous species are significantly more contextually conspicuous compared with non‐venomous species. However, while these results provide support for the link between the evolution of aposematism in relation to venom, we do not find an association with the potency or the pain‐inducing capacity of venoms with the data used in this study, indicating that these traits may not be important drivers of the evolution of aposematism in snakes. Our novel approach demonstrates how incorporating the environmental context of a species can shed light on our understanding of the evolution of conspicuous colouration.
necee3e673f88: Introgression between genetically distinct populations generates variation that may promote adaptation to diverse environmental conditions. In the mosquito Aedes aegypti, the forest‐associated subspecies Aedes aegypti formosus (Aaf) underwent a domestication process approximately 5000 years ago, giving rise to the globally invasive, human‐associated arbovirus vector Aedes aegypti aegypti (Aaa). Despite extensive human‐mediated transport, the two subspecies remain largely distinct, with admixture documented mainly in coastal Africa and Saudi Arabia. We examined Saudi Arabian Ae. aegypti across climatically contrasting regions – the humid south and arid west‐ using a Saudi Arabian dataset (11,939 SNPs) to examine within‐country genetic and environmental variation and a global dataset (13,455 SNPs) to assess ancestry and admixture in a worldwide context. Genomic analyses revealed strong west–south differentiation, with Jazan Highland showing admixture between subspecies and the highest proportion of Aaf ancestry. Multiple pulses of gene flow into and within southern Saudi Arabia suggest Aaf populations act as a reservoir of genetic variation. Genome‐wide scans identified a candidate region associated with the humidity gradient, harbouring an elongase of very long‐chain fatty acids (AAEL024147), essential for cuticle production and minimizing water loss. Because the Saudi Arabian genetic background is predominantly the arid‐adapted subspecies Aaa, the presence of Aaf ancestry at this locus may reflect localized introgression with adaptive relevance under an increasingly humid environment. Our findings highlight how secondary contact between divergent lineages may contribute to local adaptation in Ae. aegypti, with implications for predicting responses to environmental change.
n048a4b606033: Many of the most challenging decisions facing natural resource managers today can be understood as time dependent. The concept of time‐dependent decisions is useful when considering natural resource management decisions that are characterized by nonstationarity in the underlying ecological system, uncertainty surrounding key ecological relationships, efficacy of management interventions, and difficult trade‐offs between the present and the future. In a time‐dependent decision, the optimal action changes depending on when the decision is made. We surveyed literature from the fields of cognitive psychology, environmental decision‐making, and natural resource management to identify a key set of cognitive and institutional barriers that prevent decision makers from recognizing their decisions as time dependent. This failure obscures the complexity of nonstationarity, uncertainty, and intertemporal choice in natural resource management and facilitates assumptions of stationarity and time independence. We used land acquisition in the context of climate change as an example to explore the barriers to effective time‐dependent decision‐making at both individual and institutional scales. Using a theoretical model of land acquisition, we quantified the value of accounting for time dependence by comparing the performance of time‐dependent, nonstationary decision models with models that assume time independence and stationarity. We found that the conservation value of land acquisition decisions was significantly improved through the use of time‐dependent optimization models and that this improvement increased as nonstationarity increased. Finally, explicitly recognizing the time dependence of many natural resource management decisions will help improve the utility of existing decision tools and frameworks. Barreras cognitivas e institucionales para la gestión efectiva de recursos naturales bajo el cambio global Resumen Muchas de las decisiones más complejas a las que se enfrentan hoy en día los gestores de recursos naturales pueden entenderse como dependientes del tiempo. El concepto de decisiones dependientes del tiempo resulta útil a la hora de analizar las decisiones de gestión de recursos naturales que se caracterizan por un sistema ecológico subyacente no estacionario, la incertidumbre en torno a las relaciones ecológicas clave, la eficacia de las intervenciones de gestión y las difíciles disyuntivas entre el presente y el futuro. En una decisión dependiente del tiempo, la acción óptima varía en función del momento en que se toma la decisión. Revisamos la bibliografía de los campos de la psicología cognitiva, la toma de decisiones ambientales y la gestión de recursos naturales para identificar un conjunto clave de barreras cognitivas e institucionales que impiden a los responsables de la toma de decisiones reconocer que sus decisiones dependen del tiempo. Este fallo oculta la complejidad de algo no estacionario, la incertidumbre y la elección intertemporal en la gestión de los recursos naturales y favorece la adopción de supuestos de algo estacionario e independencia temporal. Utilizamos la adquisición de terrenos en el contexto del cambio climático como ejemplo para explorar las barreras que impiden una toma de decisiones eficaz dependiente del tiempo, tanto a escala individual como institucional. Mediante un modelo teórico de adquisición de terrenos, cuantificamos el valor de tener en cuenta la dependencia temporal comparando el rendimiento de los modelos de decisión no estacionarios y dependientes del tiempo con los modelos que asumen independencia temporal y ser estacionario. Constatamos que el valor de conservación de las decisiones de adquisición de terrenos mejoraba significativamente mediante el uso de modelos de optimización dependientes del tiempo y que esta mejora aumentaba a medida que aumentaba lo no estacionario.…
n0e37783dbac2: Microplastic accumulation is an increasingly widespread anthropogenic disturbance in agricultural soils, yet ecological risk assessments remain dominated by simplified laboratory assays that may not capture context‐dependent responses under field conditions. Here, we combined a five‐year experiment across four semi‐arid cropland sites with a global synthesis restricted exclusively to outdoor field observations to quantify microplastic effects on crop yield, soil quality, and ecosystem multifunctionality. Under a high microplastic loading (0.2% w/w), we detected no consistent negative functional responses across crops, sites, and growing years. The field‐only synthesis revealed weak average effects but substantial cross‐study heterogeneity. Plant presence was associated with weaker effects, with vegetated systems showing milder changes in soil quality and ecosystem multifunctionality than plant‐free soils. Biodegradable polymers did not show a consistent ecological advantage over conventional polymers across field settings. Our findings indicate that effects inferred primarily from laboratory studies cannot be directly extrapolated to the field scale. Importantly, weak functional responses do not address crop internal microplastic uptake, dietary exposure, or toxicological risk, which require separate assessment. These results provide a more realistic basis for assessing the consequences of microplastic pollution for agricultural ecosystem functioning and resilience under global change.
nc7f30d21b4be: A multi‐proxy approach integrating radial growth, leaf morphology, stable isotopes, elemental composition and soil properties revealed interacting mechanisms underlying drought‐induced dieback in Mediterranean pine populations. Declining trees showed stronger drought impacts on growth, altered stomatal regulation, nutrient imbalances and accelerated senescence, with distinct species‐specific patterns. These responses highlight interconnected carbon–water, nutritional and edaphic constraints driving tree vigour decline. Abstract Drought‐induced tree mortality is a complex process involving interdependent shifts in tree water, carbon and nutrient relations, alongside adjustments in growth and trait variability. Anticipating dieback under increasing drought severity requires mechanistic insights into the underlying physiological processes. We applied a tree‐level, multi‐proxy approach to identify factors associated with vigour decline in mortality hotspots of Mediterranean Pinus sylvestris, Pinus pinaster and Pinus halepensis forests located in north‐eastern Spain. Tree‐ring metrics, foliar carbon and oxygen stable isotopes (δ13C, ∆18O) and elemental composition and soil properties were integrated to assess drought impact on growth (DGIi), intrinsic water‐use efficiency (iWUE), ∆18O‐inferred stomatal conductance (G∆18O) and nutrient status of trees. Declining trees had consistently higher DGIi than non‐declining trees. In P. sylvestris and P. pinaster, elevated DGIi was linked to reduced G∆18O and increased iWUE, indicating more severe drought stress in declining trees. Declining P. sylvestris and P. halepensis also exhibited pronounced nutrient imbalances—particularly in P, K, Zn, Fe, S and Ca—and all species showed disrupted Fe:Cu ratios. Differences in vigour across species were also associated with variation in needle size and morphology, tree height and soil pH, with declining P. sylvestris and P. halepensis displaying contrasting adjustments in leaf mass per area. Synthesis. Together, these results highlight that interactions among hydraulic impairment, nutrient imbalance, foliar senescence and unfavourable soil conditions amplify climatic stress in the studied populations of Mediterranean pines. Such potential feedbacks may accelerate crown defoliation and ultimately contribute to tree death under increasing drought severity.
n98659e2a1126: Shrub canopies create microrefuges for recruit diversity. Across 10 Mediterranean shrublands, recruits beneath canopies encompassed a wider range of climatic niches and greater phylogenetic diversity than those in open ground. By hosting diverse climatic strategies, plant canopies may help sustain biodiversity under climate change, offering a management strategy that lets nature select future winners rather than relying on uncertain climate forecasts. Abstract Plant performance has a climatic optimum, especially during early establishment, and declines when conditions deviate from this optimum. However, shrubs can buffer unfavourable climatic conditions by creating more suitable microclimates beneath their canopies, facilitating the establishment of species with disparate climatic niches. Across 10 Mediterranean shrubland sites, we compared climatic niche disparity and phylogenetic structure of plant recruits under shrub canopies versus open ground, integrating environmental, niche and phylogenetic data to reveal underlying abiotic and evolutionary drivers. We show in 10 Mediterranean shrublands that the climatic niche disparity of recruits established under shrub canopies is significantly greater than that of those in open ground. This pattern was only weakly associated with shrub‐driven microenvironmental heterogeneity, estimated using variability in photosynthetically active radiation as a coarse proxy, suggesting that additional abiotic factors may also contribute to recruit niche disparity. In addition, recruit assemblages beneath shrubs were composed, on average, of more distantly related species. Combined with phylogenetic conservatism in the aridity‐response axis of their climatic niche, this pattern results in the co‐occurrence of recruits with higher disparity in key climatic niche axes beneath canopies. Synthesis. Plant canopies host recruit species that exhibit a wide diversity of climatic niches, which may play a role in maintaining biodiversity under ongoing and future climate change.
na3d44d29b8b4: Understanding biodiversity patterns requires integrating information across the interrelated dimensions that organize life. Species occupy specific regions in geographic space, respond to environmental conditions and vary within attribute (or trait) spaces that are shaped by their ecological and evolutionary histories. However, most analyses address these dimensions independently, limiting our ability to understand how constraints in one space interrelate to patterns in another. Developing approaches that explicitly quantify and connect the geometry of these spaces should unify the study of biodiversity across scales and dimensions. We implement such a framework in the letsR R package by constructing a triad of presence–absence matrices (PAMs) representing geographic, environmental and attribute spaces. A concise set of functions computes geometry‐aware descriptors such as centrality, frequency, isolation and border proximity, and allows these descriptors to be propagated among spaces through explicit connectors. This design builds on the letsR architecture and integrates with functions to facilitate macroecological analysis. Using global terrestrial mammals as a model group, we illustrate how descriptors derived from environmental space can be mapped back into geographic and attribute spaces. This approach reveals where particular regions of climatic space are common or rare, how isolated they are and how these properties influence species richness across dimensions. This novel implementation lowers the barrier to reproducible, geometry‐aware analyses and enables direct tests of how constraints in one space influence diversity in others, advancing a more integrated understanding of macroecological and macroevolutionary patterns. Resumo Compreender os padrões de biodiversidade requer considerar conjuntamente as diferentes dimensões que organizam a distribuição e a diversidade da vida. Em cada uma dessas dimensões, as espécies ocupam posições particulares que refletem suas histórias ecológicas e evolutivas: distribuem‐se em determinadas regiões geográficas, estão associadas a diferentes condições ambientais e apresentam combinações específicas de atributos. Ainda assim, essas dimensões são frequentemente analisadas de forma isolada, o que limita nossa capacidade de compreender como as restrições que atuam em um espaço se refletem nos padrões observados em outros. Abordagens capazes de quantificar e relacionar explicitamente a geometria desses diferentes espaços podem, portanto, contribuir para uma visão mais integrada da biodiversidade, abrangendo diferentes escalas e dimensões. Neste trabalho, implementamos esse arcabouço metodológico no pacote letsR para a linguagem R, a partir da construção de uma tríade de matrizes de presença e ausência (PAMs) que representam os espaços geográfico, ambiental e de atributos. As funções do pacote permitem calcular descritores que levam em conta a geometria desses espaços, incluindo centralidade, frequência, isolamento e proximidade às bordas. Esses descritores podem então ser transferidos entre os diferentes espaços por meio de conexões explícitas entre as matrizes. A implementação aproveita a arquitetura já existente do letsR e se integra às demais funções do pacote voltadas à análise macroecológica. Utilizando os mamíferos terrestres do mundo como grupo modelo, mostramos como descritores obtidos no espaço ambiental podem ser projetados nos espaços geográfico e de atributos. Essa abordagem permite identificar quais regiões do espaço climático são mais comuns ou mais raras, avaliar seu grau de isolamento e investigar de que forma essas propriedades se associam aos padrões de riqueza de espécies nas diferentes dimensões consideradas. Essa nova implementação torna mais acessível a realização de análises reprodutíveis que incorporam explicitamente a geometria dos diferentes espaços ecológicos e biogeográficos.…
nc3d1f238f903: Gene Ontology (GO) enrichment analysis has been widely adopted for interpretating omics data, including in ecological research. Although valuable for summarizing large gene lists into functional categories, it is often treated as the final interpretive step. In ecological omics, where functional annotations are frequently incomplete and experimental validation is often difficult, this reliance can lead to repetitive, generic conclusions that lack environmental and mechanistic specificity. Although previous literature has addressed the statistical and annotation‐related limitations of GO enrichment, its role in shaping the broader interpretive process has received less critical attention. Here, we highlight a conceptual weakness: the treatment of enriched GO terms as definitive biological insight. We focus particularly on ecological studies of non‐model organisms in complex, and heterogeneous environments. We discuss complementary strategies, including co‐expression network analysis, integration with environmental metadata, phylogenetically informed annotation, and AI‐assisted functional inference. To promote more context‐sensitive interpretation, we introduce the concept of GO‐Deep, which frames GO enrichment as a starting point for integrative, multilayered functional insight. By reframing GO enrichment as an entry point rather than a conclusion, ecological omics can move toward more mechanistically informative and environmentally grounded interpretations of high‐throughput data.
n696501fb3fb2: Protists are the dominant eukaryotes in the ocean biosphere, and oceanic protists (OP) serve as a critical link among bacterial production, primary producers, and higher trophic levels. This study examined the community structure and vertical organization of OP assemblages in the Bay of Bengal (BoB) across three depth layers: surface (5 m), mid‐depth (150 m), and bottom (300 m). Multivariate ordination, diversity metrics, and network analyses consistently demonstrated that vertical depth is the primary factor structuring OP communities, whereas regional (north–south) variability was minimal. Alpha diversity analyses showed that Shannon and Simpson diversity differed significantly among depth layers, whereas Chao1 richness did not, indicating that depth‐related changes were reflected mainly in community evenness and dominance structure rather than estimated richness. Beta diversity analyses (PERMANOVA) further confirmed strong depth‐wise separation of communities and no significant regional effect. Surface OP communities were characterized mainly by Syndiniales, with additional contributions from Polycystinea, Dinophyceae, Diatomea, Intramacronucleata, and Prymnesiales, whereas mid‐depth and bottom assemblages showed stronger contributions from Polycystinea and Diplonemea. Network analyses revealed depth‐specific differences in modularity, connectivity, and robustness, with the mid‐depth network showing the highest modularity and the bottom network showing the strongest local connectivity but greater sensitivity to node removal. RDA highlighted clear depth‐related associations between OP communities and environmental gradients, with surface assemblages aligned with temperature and Chl‐a, and deeper assemblages associated with salinity, phosphate, and silicic acid gradients. Overall, these findings reveal a vertically stratified organization of OP communities in the BoB, associated with depth‐dependent environmental gradients and potential biotic associations within a stratified tropical ocean system.
n0a5ef150f4b5: The global understanding of the functioning of Mesozoic marine ecosystems has historically been heavily biased toward paleoecological models based on Northern Hemisphere localities with exceptional preservation; meanwhile, highly fossiliferous Western Gondwana sites remained poorly addressed. To contribute to filling this gap, this study provides the first integrated, multi-trophic paleoecological reconstruction of both marine macroinvertebrate and vertebrate associations in Western Gondwana. We synthesize and analyze two age- and stratigraphically constrained taxonomic datasets from different paleogeographic positions over the carbonate ramp of the Vaca Muerta Formation (Neuquén Basin, Argentina): the Sierra de la Cara Cura and Cerro Lotena sections. The data obtained enabled us to evaluate ecosystem dynamics using quantitative and qualitative tools, including Westermann Morphospace modeling, multi-level benthic tiering, and vertebrate trophic-guild analyses. The results reveal a complex, vertically stratified pelagic realm that remained functionally stable for over nine million years. The vertebrate assemblage is abundant and taxonomically diverse, including top predators and more specialized forms. Actinopterygian fishes, particularly, displayed a wide range of body shapes, locomotor modes, and feeding strategies, spanning pelagic to demersal/benthic habitats and encompassing suspension-feeding, invertivorous, microphagous, piscivorous, and durophagous forms. Mesopredatory marine reptiles’ morphological disparity suggests strict niche partitioning despite preying upon similar food sources. Ammonite communities tracked a shallowing-upward trend, shifting from early Tithonian streamlined, demersal active swimmers into heavily sculptured planktonic drifters mechanically adapted to storm-dominated environments. Conversely, the benthic realm dynamics remained decoupled from the water column and were strictly regulated by oxygenation, water energy, and substrate consistency variations. Benthic invertebrate ecosystems shifted from highly impoverished, opportunistic, or pseudoplanktic communities during the early Tithonian into highly diversified, multi-tiered assemblages punctuated by extensive oyster biostromes as oxygenation improved by the late Berriasian, before a final shallowing trend led to a major ecological reorganization at the Intravalanginian Discontinuity. Direct and indirect evidence on biotic interactions reveal a highly interconnected, complex trophic network, spanning microplanktonic producers to hypercarnivorous reptile apex predators. Ultimately, these findings highlight the coordinated eco-spatial and trophic mechanisms of Gondwanan ecosystems and establish the Neuquén Basin as a critical window into global marine dynamics during the Jurassic–Cretaceous transition.
n5164e415cc3b: Read the free Plain Language Summary for this article on the Journal blog. Abstract Charles Elton proposed that species‐rich communities are more resistant to invasion, yet a well‐known paradox persists: native diversity suppresses invasion at small scales while correlating positively with non‐native species diversity at broad scales. Moving beyond native observed diversity alone to community completeness, defined as the ratio of native observed diversity to its specific species pool, may offer a potential framework to address this scale dependency. This is because the completeness index reflects the degree to which a habitat saturates its available niche space, shaped jointly by abiotic and biotic filtering in an origin‐blind manner. At small spatial scales, native observed diversity and dark diversity (suitable yet absent native species) are negatively correlated. This implies that high native observed diversity indicates high community completeness, leaving limited vacant niche opportunities for both un‐arrived native and non‐native species and thus reducing invasibility. In contrast, at large spatial scales, greater environmental heterogeneity can yield a vastly expanded regional species pool where dark diversity also accumulates more, potentially resulting in lower community completeness and heightened susceptibility. It should be noted that native community completeness, based on the extant species pool, fails to capture the niche spaces left by historical species losses—a gap tracked by temporal dark diversity dynamics—yet these hypervolume holes can instead be successfully exploited and predicted by non‐native community completeness. Following on this logic, I propose a Completeness‐Based Invasion Theory, which hypothesizes that community invasibility is inversely related to community completeness across spatial scales. While further empirical testing across diverse systems is required, measuring completeness alongside observed diversity may provide a novel, scale‐independent perspective to advance our understanding and management of biological invasions. Combining both native community completeness and non‐native community completeness to predict non‐native species invasions may currently represent the optimal approach. n2bcf69ef1b8c: Read the free Plain Language Summary for this article on the Journal blog. Abstract Restoring the soil microbiome is increasingly recognized as an important requirement for the success of ecosystem restoration. Soil inoculation can reintroduce the missing taxa, but its application is limited by the large amount of donor soil that is needed and by the poor persistence of the inoculants, because of habitat filtering, priority effects and the loss of plant–microbe feedbacks. Here we propose the metabolite‐inoculum approach, a framework that combines the chemical diversity of plants with soil inoculation, in order to improve the establishment, persistence and effectiveness of introduced microbial communities. In this framework, the chemical input is delivered as fresh and dead plant material, as extracts of this material or as purified compounds that are applied together with the inoculum, and not by adding or manipulating the living plant community. We first synthesize the evidence that plant metabolites, from both above‐ and below‐ground tissues, act as selective regulators of soil microbial composition and diversity. Building on this, we propose a framework for the selection of plant materials and metabolites at the species, tissue and compound levels, and we introduce the parallel concepts of core and keystone metabolites that are matched to their corresponding microbial groups. We then identify the main challenges of the approach, the mismatch in timescale, the non‐target effects and the feasibility, and we translate them into testable hypotheses. Finally, we discuss the contexts in which the approach is likely to work and the contexts in which it is not. In this way, we frame the metabolite‐inoculum approach as a research agenda through bridging chemical ecology and microbial ecology, offering a potential solution to reduce dependency on donor soil, improve inoculant effectiveness and accelerate the recovery of degraded soils toward desired ecosystem states. n0c315cf546c6: Read the free Plain Language Summary for this article on the Journal blog. Abstract The rhizosphere microbiome is critical for forest ecological functions, yet the mechanisms through which tree species identity and neighbour tree interactions are associated with its assembly remain poorly understood. Using Illumina MiSeq and liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry (LC–MS), we investigated how tree species (pine vs. liquidambar) and forest composition (pure vs. mixed) shape rhizosphere microbial communities and root metabolites in subtropical forests. Rhizosphere fungal community structure differed significantly across rhizosphere types, whereas bacterial community and metabolite profiles differed primarily between the pure pine forest and other forest types. Predicted functional shifts included a decline in cellulolytic bacteria (−27%) and an increase in denitrifying groups (+54%), with ectomycorrhizal fungi enriched in mixed than pure forests (p < 0.05). Metabolite profiling revealed that lipids, organic acids and sugars were the most abundant compound classes, with 55 metabolites differentially abundant between pure pine and mixed forest rhizospheres. Rhizosphere metabolite profiles were significantly correlated with microbial community structure (p < 0.05). Specific microbe–metabolite associations were identified; fatty acids positively correlated with oligotrophic bacteria (WPS‐2), sugars with denitrifiers (Reyranella) and dipeptides with the beneficial fungus Penicillium. These results demonstrate that tree species identity is associated with rhizosphere microbiome assembly via root metabolite‐associated feedbacks, which correlate with soil nutrient cycling. This provides a mechanistic, function‐oriented framework for understanding plant–microbiome interaction and harnessing them to enhance ecosystem resilience.
